weeks.context:
Before containers, Kubernetes, or Terraform, you need to understand what a server is: a computer running software that listens for network connections and responds to them. Strip away all the abstraction, and that is the whole thing. This week you operate a raw Linux server without any help from managed platforms. Everything you do manually this week is something you will later automate, but you cannot automate what you do not understand.

A VPS (Virtual Private Server) is a slice of a physical server running as an isolated virtual machine. You get root access. There is no UI. You interact via SSH. The operating system is Linux (Ubuntu is the standard choice, large community, long-term support releases, most documentation assumes it). You are responsible for everything: updates, firewall rules, web server configuration, process management.

SSH (Secure Shell) is how you connect. You authenticate with a key pair (more secure than a password). The private key stays on your machine; the public key goes on the server. When you SSH, you prove you have the private key without ever sending it.

What a web server is: nginx or Apache listens on port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). When a request arrives, it reads the request line (GET / HTTP/1.1), the Host header (which domain is being requested), and routes the request to the appropriate application (a Node process, a static file, a Python app). The web server is a reverse proxy, it sits in front of your application and handles the HTTP protocol details.

Process management: your Node.js application is a process. If it crashes, you want it to restart automatically. systemd is the Linux init system that manages processes, it can start a service on boot, restart it on crash, and provide logs. This week you manage your Node process with systemd.

The capstone project for this track is Edge Portfolio: a portfolio site deployed on real infrastructure, progressively hardened over the first 4 weeks.

items.title: SQL, the language your data lives in
items.body:
## What SQL is
SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to relational databases, Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, BigQuery, Snowflake. Every analyst, data engineer, backend dev, ML engineer reads + writes SQL daily.

There is ONE syntax (with minor dialect quirks). Learn it once; use it on every database for the rest of your career.

## The five queries that cover 80% of real work
```sql
-- 1. SELECT: pull rows from a table
SELECT name, email FROM users;

-- 2. WHERE: filter rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE country = 'GM' AND age >= 18;

-- 3. ORDER BY + LIMIT: sort + cap
SELECT name, signup_at FROM users ORDER BY signup_at DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 4. GROUP BY: aggregate (counts, sums, averages per group)
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS n FROM users GROUP BY country;

-- 5. JOIN: combine rows from two tables
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.total > 100;
```

## Mental model
Every query is `SELECT <columns> FROM <table> [WHERE <filter>] [GROUP BY ...] [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...]`. Memorise that skeleton; everything else is variation.

## Try it without setup
Practice these queries right now at https://sqlbolt.com/lesson/select_queries_introduction, interactive, no install, 15 minutes to read through the first 5 lessons.

## When you'll see SQL next
This track uses SQL whenever it touches a database. The five queries above are your bedrock.

items.title: What this environment is, and why before anything else
items.body:
## What it is
DevOps work happens in a terminal. You'll spend hours in it, running git commands, ssh-ing into servers, applying Terraform, watching CI output. If you're not comfortable opening a terminal and running a command, every later week is harder than it needs to be.

Three things you must have by the end of today:
1. A terminal you can open and navigate (Anaconda Prompt or PowerShell on Windows; Terminal on Mac/Linux).
2. **Git** installed and configured with your name + email.
3. A **GitHub** account, with `git push` working from your laptop to a test repo.

## Why before anything else
Every project on this track gets pushed to GitHub. Every Terraform run is committed to git. Every CI/CD pipeline starts with `git push`. Skip this day and Week 1 falls over the first time you're told to push.

## What you'll do today
Install git, configure name + email, create a GitHub account, clone an empty test repo, make a commit, push it. Then you're ready for the rest of the week.

days.title: What is the cloud?
days.summary: Watch and write today.

items.title: What 'the cloud' and infrastructure-as-code actually are
items.body:
## What it is
'The cloud' is someone else's computers, rented by the minute, controlled over an API. AWS owns the data centres; you rent a slice and pay only for what you use. There is no physical machine you touch, you describe what you want and AWS provisions it.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the practice of declaring that infrastructure in text files instead of clicking through a web console. You write a file that says 'I want an S3 bucket and a CloudFront distribution', and a tool (Terraform) makes reality match the file.

## Why it matters
Clicking around the AWS console works once. But you cannot review a click, diff a click, or roll back a click. With IaC:
- The infra is **version-controlled**, every change is a git commit
- It is **reproducible**, `terraform apply` rebuilds the exact same stack on a fresh account
- It is **reviewable**, a teammate reads the diff before it ships

## Where this fits in Edge Portfolio
This week you ship Edge Portfolio v0.1: a real portfolio page, served worldwide over HTTPS from AWS S3 + CloudFront, with every piece of infrastructure declared in Terraform. By Sunday it is live at a public URL and the Terraform code is on your GitHub, your first infrastructure artifact.

items.title: The shell, the filesystem, and why the terminal is the DevOps cockpit
items.body:
## What it is
The shell is a text interface to your operating system. You type a command, it runs, it prints output. Every server you will ever manage in this track has no graphical interface, the shell is the only way in.

The handful of commands that do 90% of the work:

```bash
pwd # print working directory, where am I?
ls # list files here
cd edge-portfolio # change directory
mkdir infra # make a directory
cat index.html # print a file's contents
```

## Why it matters
A web page is just a text file (`index.html`) that a server hands to a browser. Before you can deploy one, you need to (a) navigate a filesystem from the keyboard and (b) create that file. Both happen in the shell. Today you set up a working terminal and hand-write the portfolio page you will host all week.

## The mental model for HTML
`index.html` is the default file a web server serves when someone visits `/`. It is plain text with tags. The browser reads the tags and paints the page. That is the entire contract, no magic.

days.title: Sign up for AWS (safely)

items.title: AWS accounts, the root user, IAM, and not getting a surprise bill
items.body:
## What it is
An AWS account is your tenancy in Amazon's cloud. It comes with one all-powerful root user (your signup email). The first rule of AWS: lock the root user away and never use it for daily work. Instead you create an IAM user, a scoped identity for everyday tasks.

IAM (Identity and Access Management) is how AWS decides who can do what. A user has credentials (an Access Key ID + Secret) and policies (permissions). Your CLI authenticates as this IAM user.

## Why it matters, two ways beginners get burned
1. **A leaked root key = full account compromise.** Attackers scan GitHub for committed AWS keys and spin up crypto miners within minutes. MFA on root + an IAM user for daily work is the defence.
2. **A surprise bill.** A misconfigured resource can quietly run up charges. A **billing alarm** emails you the moment estimated charges cross a threshold (set it at $5). This is non-negotiable on a learner account.

## Where this fits
Today you create the account, enable MFA, set the billing alarm, create the `forge-dev` IAM user, and configure the AWS CLI. Everything Terraform does this week authenticates as that IAM user.

items.title: Safe AWS setup
items.body:
STEP 1, Sign up.
 Open the AWS signup card. Use a real email + real card. Pick 'Basic Support, Free'.

STEP 2, Turn on MFA (multi-factor auth) on the root user.
 In AWS console, click your name (top right) → Security credentials → MFA → Add.
 Use an authenticator app (Google Authenticator or Authy).

STEP 3, Set a billing alarm at $5.
 In console search bar, type 'CloudWatch' → Alarms → Create alarm → Billing → Total Estimated Charge → set threshold $5 → notify your email.
 Now if your bill ever hits $5 you get an email.

STEP 4, Create an IAM user for daily use (NEVER use root again).
 In console search bar: 'IAM' → Users → Create user.
 Username: forge-dev. Attach policy: AdministratorAccess.
 After creating, click the user → Security credentials → Create access key → 'Command line interface' → save the Access Key ID + Secret Access Key in a password manager.

STEP 5, Install AWS CLI.
 Mac: brew install awscli
 Win: download from https://aws.amazon.com/cli/
 Linux: sudo apt install awscli
 Then: aws configure
 Paste your Access Key + Secret. Region: us-east-1. Output: json.

STEP 6, Verify.
 aws sts get-caller-identity
 YOU SHOULD SEE: your IAM user ARN (not root).

days.title: Install Terraform
days.summary: Today we install Terraform and write our first .tf file.

items.title: Terraform: providers, resources, and the init / plan / apply loop
items.body:
## What it is
Terraform is the IaC tool you'll use all track. You write `.tf` files describing the desired state; Terraform figures out the API calls to make it real. Three concepts:

- **Provider**, the plugin that talks to a specific cloud (here, `aws`). You declare it once.
- **Resource**, one thing you want to exist (`aws_s3_bucket`, `aws_cloudfront_distribution`). Each has a type, a local name, and a config block.
- **State**, Terraform's record of what it has already created, so it knows what to change next time.

## The core loop
```bash
terraform init # download the provider plugin (once per project)
terraform plan # preview: what WILL change, before anything happens
terraform apply # execute the plan after you type 'yes'
```

`plan` is the safety rail, it shows you 'Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy' so you confirm intent before touching reality.

## Where this fits
Today you create your first real resource: an S3 bucket, declared in `main.tf` and applied. S3 bucket names are globally unique across all of AWS, yours must be a name no one else has used.

items.why: Click 'Open' to download. Pick your OS.

cards.prompt: `terraform plan` previews what will change WITHOUT modifying any real infrastructure.
cards.whenRight: Right, plan is read-only. It is your safety check before apply touches anything.
cards.whenWrong: plan is a dry run. Nothing changes until you run apply and type 'yes'. Always read the plan first.
cards.sim:
$ terraform plan
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

cards.prompt: S3 bucket names only need to be unique within your own AWS account.
cards.whenRight: Right, they are GLOBALLY unique across all of AWS. Pick a name no one on earth has used.
cards.whenWrong: Bucket names are globally unique across all AWS accounts worldwide. Add your name + a year to be safe.
cards.sim:
bucket = 'jane-edge-portfolio-2026'
# must be unique on all of AWS

cards.prompt: You must run `terraform init` before `terraform apply` in a new project.
cards.whenRight: Right, init downloads the provider plugin. apply fails without it on a fresh project.
cards.whenWrong: init comes first, it fetches the aws provider. Without it, Terraform doesn't know how to talk to AWS.
cards.sim:
terraform init # downloads aws provider
terraform apply # now it can run

items.title: First Terraform resource
items.body:
STEP 1, Install Terraform.
 Mac: brew install terraform
 Win: download zip, unzip, add to PATH (or use Chocolatey)
 Linux: follow the official Linux instructions
 Verify: terraform version → should print 1.x.x.

STEP 2, Make an infra folder.
 cd Desktop/edge-portfolio
 mkdir infra
 cd infra

STEP 3, Write your first main.tf.
 In VS Code, new file: edge-portfolio/infra/main.tf. Type:

 terraform {
 required_providers {
 aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
 }
 }
 provider "aws" {
 region = "us-east-1"
 }
 resource "aws_s3_bucket" "portfolio" {
 bucket = "YOUR-NAME-edge-portfolio-2026"
 }

 Replace YOUR-NAME with your real name (lowercase, no spaces). S3 bucket names are GLOBALLY unique, yours must not exist anywhere.

STEP 4, Run Terraform.
 terraform init
 YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Terraform has been successfully initialized!'
 terraform plan
 YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.'
 terraform apply
 Type 'yes' when asked.
 YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Apply complete! Resources: 1 added'

STEP 5, Verify in AWS.
 In the AWS console, search 'S3'. You see your bucket. Your first cloud resource.

days.title: Add CloudFront in front of S3
days.summary: Today we add a CDN so your site loads fast from anywhere in the world.

items.title: CloudFront, CDNs, and serving a static site fast + private
items.body:
## What it is
S3 stores your files. CloudFront is AWS's CDN (Content Delivery Network), a global fleet of edge servers that cache your content close to users. A visitor in Tokyo hits a Tokyo edge node, not your bucket's home region. Result: fast loads everywhere.

Two pieces make this secure and correct:
- **Origin Access Identity (OAI)**, lets CloudFront read your S3 bucket while keeping the bucket itself **private**. Users can only reach files through CloudFront, never the raw bucket URL.
- **`viewer_protocol_policy = redirect-to-https`**, anyone arriving over HTTP is bounced to HTTPS automatically.

## Why it matters
Serving straight from a public S3 bucket is slow (one region) and exposes the bucket. The S3 + CloudFront + OAI pattern is the industry-standard way to host a static site: fast, private origin, HTTPS by default. You'll reuse this exact pattern for years.

## Where this fits
Today `main.tf` grows from one bucket to the full stack: bucket + OAI + bucket policy + CloudFront distribution, with an `output` that prints your live `https://...cloudfront.net` URL. CloudFront takes 5-10 minutes to deploy globally, that wait is normal.

cards.prompt: A CDN like CloudFront speeds up your site by caching content on edge servers near users.
cards.whenRight: Right, a visitor hits the nearest edge node, not your origin region. That's the whole point of a CDN.
cards.whenWrong: That is exactly what a CDN does. Edge caching means a user in Tokyo loads from Tokyo, not Virginia.
cards.sim:
User (Tokyo) -> CloudFront edge (Tokyo)
# fast, cached, origin untouched

cards.prompt: An Origin Access Identity (OAI) lets you keep the S3 bucket private while CloudFront still serves it.
cards.whenRight: Exactly, OAI is the bridge. Bucket stays private; only CloudFront can read it.
cards.whenWrong: OAI is what keeps the bucket private. CloudFront reads via OAI; the public can't hit the raw bucket URL.
cards.sim:
Public -> CloudFront -> (OAI) -> private S3
# raw bucket URL: access denied

cards.prompt: CloudFront distributions deploy instantly, if your URL 404s right after apply, something is broken.
cards.whenRight: Right, global deploy takes 5-10 minutes. A brief 404 right after apply is expected; wait it out.
cards.whenWrong: CloudFront takes 5-10 min to propagate to all edges. An immediate 404 is normal, give it time before debugging.

items.title: Git, .gitignore, and why Terraform state must never be committed
items.body:
## What it is
Today the Terraform code itself becomes a portfolio piece on GitHub. But not every file belongs in git. Terraform produces local files you must exclude:

```text
.terraform/ # downloaded provider binaries (huge)
*.tfstate # the state file, may contain secrets
*.tfstate.backup
.terraform.lock.hcl # (often committed; fine either way for solo)
```

## Why it matters
The state file (`terraform.tfstate`) records what Terraform created, and can contain sensitive values (resource IDs, sometimes secrets). Committing it to a public repo leaks information and creates merge conflicts on teams. The `.gitignore` is what keeps it out.

A good README turns raw `.tf` files into a story a recruiter understands: what it builds, the live URL, the cost, and how someone forks and deploys it themselves. The README is the difference between 'some config files' and 'a portfolio piece'.

## Where this fits
Today you add `.gitignore`, write the README, and push Edge Portfolio's infrastructure to a public GitHub repo. The repo, not just the live site, is the deliverable.

items.title: GitHub, create new repository
items.why: Click 'Open'. Name: edge-portfolio. Public.

cards.prompt: Terraform state files (*.tfstate) should be added to .gitignore and never committed to a public repo.
cards.whenRight: Right, state can contain secrets and resource IDs. Keep it out of git, especially public repos.
cards.whenWrong: State files can leak secrets and cause team conflicts. Always .gitignore *.tfstate.
cards.sim:
# .gitignore
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.backup
.terraform/

cards.prompt: A README that explains what the project builds, its cost, and how to deploy it makes the repo a real portfolio piece.
cards.whenRight: Exactly, the README turns config files into a story a recruiter can follow and trust.
cards.whenWrong: The README is what communicates value. Without it, even great IaC looks like noise to a reviewer.

cards.prompt: Committing the `.terraform/` directory is good practice because it makes the repo self-contained.
cards.whenRight: Right, it holds large downloaded provider binaries. `terraform init` re-fetches them; never commit it.
cards.whenWrong: Never commit .terraform/, it's big downloaded binaries. Anyone who clones runs `terraform init` to get them.

days.title: Test the destroy + redeploy
days.summary: Today you test what real engineers test: can you wipe and rebuild from scratch?

items.title: Idempotency: the destroy + redeploy test that proves your IaC works
items.body:
## What it is
The real test of infrastructure-as-code is not 'does the site load?', it is 'can I wipe everything and rebuild it identically from the code alone?'

```bash
terraform destroy # tear down every resource in state
terraform apply # rebuild it all from main.tf
```

If your site comes back identical after a full destroy + redeploy, your IaC is complete, nothing important lives only in your memory or in a manual console click.

## Why it matters, idempotency
Idempotent means running the same operation repeatedly gives the same result. Good infrastructure code is idempotent: `apply` on an unchanged file changes nothing; a destroy + apply reproduces the exact stack. This is what lets teams rebuild a region after an outage, spin up identical staging environments, and trust that the code IS the system.

If something breaks during the rebuild, you found a gap in your code, a manual step you forgot to capture. Finding it now, on a portfolio project, is far cheaper than finding it during a real incident.

## Where this fits
Today you destroy Edge Portfolio entirely, redeploy it from the Terraform code, and confirm the live URL works again. That round-trip is the proof that closes v0.1.

cards.prompt: Running `terraform destroy` then `terraform apply` should rebuild your infrastructure identically if your IaC is complete.

items.title: Destroy and redeploy
items.body:
STEP 1, Take down everything.
 cd Desktop/edge-portfolio/infra
 terraform destroy
 Type 'yes'. All AWS resources are deleted.

STEP 2, Verify the site is GONE.
 Visit your CloudFront URL, it should now error.

STEP 3, Rebuild from scratch.
 terraform apply
 Type 'yes'. Wait 10 minutes for CloudFront.
 Re-upload index.html: aws s3 cp ../index.html s3://YOUR-BUCKET/

STEP 4, Site is BACK.
 Open the new CloudFront URL (it changed!). Update your README with the new URL.
 Push the README update:
 git add README.md && git commit -m "Update CloudFront URL after redeploy" && git push

PASS CRITERIA, Edge Portfolio v0.1 ships when:
 ☐ main.tf creates S3 + CloudFront + OAI + bucket policy
 ☐ Live CloudFront URL serves your portfolio over HTTPS
 ☐ terraform destroy + terraform apply works clean (reproducible)
 ☐ Public GitHub repo named edge-portfolio
 ☐ README has the live URL + how-to-fork instructions
 ☐ .gitignore excludes .terraform/ and *.tfstate

mastery_questions: You connect to your server via SSH and run ps aux. You see your Node app is running. You also see nginx. Describe the relationship between these two processes when a user visits your website. A user's browser sends a TCP request to your server's IP on port 80 or 443. nginx is listening on those ports, it receives the request. Based on its configuration (the server_name directive matching the requested domain), nginx forwards the request to your Node app (running on port 3000, for example) via proxy_pass http://localhost:3000. The Node app processes the request and sends a response back to nginx. nginx forwards the response to the user's browser. nginx is the front door; Node is the application behind it.

Your Node application crashes. A minute later, a user visits the site and gets a 502 Bad Gateway error from nginx. What is happening and how do you prevent automatic recovery? 502 Bad Gateway means nginx cannot connect to the upstream (your Node process). The process is gone. To restart it automatically, run it as a systemd service with Restart=on-failure in the service unit file. When Node crashes, systemd detects the exit and restarts the process within seconds. You configure a restart delay (RestartSec=5) to prevent a fast crash loop. Check the logs: journalctl -u your-service-name.

You want to restrict SSH access to your server so only your IP address can connect. How do you do this and what is the risk? Configure ufw (the Ubuntu firewall): ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 22, then ufw deny 22. This allows SSH only from your IP. The risk: if your IP changes (many home ISPs assign dynamic IPs), you are locked out. The mitigation: configure ufw before locking it down, ensure you have a recovery method (DigitalOcean/Hetzner console access that does not use SSH), and use a static IP or VPN if your IP changes frequently.

Explain what happens when you run sudo apt upgrade on your server. apt downloads the new package versions for all installed software from Ubuntu's package repositories. It installs them, replacing the old versions. For services like nginx, the service is restarted automatically after the upgrade. For the kernel, a reboot is required to load the new kernel. Security patches are released regularly, a server that has not been updated in 6 months is a server with known, unpatched vulnerabilities. Set up automatic security updates: sudo dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades.
ai_assist: "Write a systemd service unit file for a Node.js application running as user 'appuser', working directory /home/appuser/app, command: node server.js. It should restart on failure with a 5-second delay, load environment variables from /etc/app/env, and start after the network is available."

"Write an nginx server block configuration for a Node.js app on port 3000. It should: listen on port 80, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, listen on port 443 with SSL cert paths, proxy requests to localhost:3000, set proxy headers (X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For), and serve static files from /home/appuser/app/public directly."

"Write a bash server hardening script for Ubuntu 22.04 that: creates a non-root user with sudo, disables root SSH login, disables password authentication, configures ufw to allow only SSH/HTTP/HTTPS, enables unattended-upgrades, and installs fail2ban."
weeks.pre_flight: Create an account on DigitalOcean, Hetzner, or Linode. Provision the smallest Ubuntu 22.04 LTS server (1 vCPU, 1GB RAM). Configure SSH key authentication (do not enable password auth). Note the server's IP address. Install nginx: sudo apt update && sudo apt install nginx. Know basic Linux commands: ls, cd, cat, sudo, systemctl, nano/vim. Read the SSH man page (man ssh) for key-based authentication.
common_mistakes: Leaving root SSH enabled with a password. Bots scan the internet and attempt to brute-force SSH passwords. Disable password authentication (PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config). Use key-based auth only. Create a non-root user with sudo for daily operations.

Running your application as root. If the application has a vulnerability and is exploited, the attacker runs as root, they own the server. Create a dedicated user for your application with no sudo privileges.

Not configuring a firewall on day one. A fresh server exposes all ports by default. Run ufw allow 22, ufw allow 80, ufw allow 443, then ufw enable. Deny everything else. Every open port is an attack surface.

Making manual changes without documentation. "I changed something in nginx.conf last month and now I do not know why that line is there." Treat configuration files as code, commit them to a git repository. This is the foundation of "infrastructure as code."

Storing application secrets in environment variables set manually on the server. These are lost if the server is destroyed. Store configuration in a file (/etc/app/env) owned by root and readable by the app user, committed to version control without the secrets (use a template with placeholder values).
weeks.debug_help: SSH connection refused: check that the server is running (DigitalOcean console). Check that sshd is running: systemctl status ssh. Check ufw rules: ufw status. If you locked yourself out, use the hosting provider's web console. nginx returns 502: check that your application process is running (systemctl status your-app). Check nginx logs: tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log. Check your app logs: journalctl -u your-app -f. DNS not pointing to server: new DNS records take 24-48 hours to propagate. Check current DNS resolution: dig your-domain.com A. Use a TTL checker to see what the world sees vs what you just set. systemd service does not start: check the service file syntax with systemctl cat your-app.service. Check the failure reason: journalctl -u your-app --since "1 hour ago".
stretch: Set up a second server and configure nginx as a load balancer between the two application servers. The upstream block in nginx distributes requests round-robin. Test by stopping one server and verifying requests still succeed. This is horizontal scaling in its simplest form.

Configure log rotation for your application logs. Without rotation, log files grow until they fill the disk. logrotate is the standard tool, configure it to rotate daily, keep 7 days of logs, and compress old logs.

Set up a simple monitoring script: a cron job that pings your website every 5 minutes and sends an email (via sendmail or a simple SMTP library) if the response code is not 200. This is primitive uptime monitoring, the concept you will replace with Prometheus and Grafana in W19.

weeks.title: Edge Portfolio v0.2: Custom domain + HTTPS
weeks.context:
A server with an IP address works, but users do not navigate to IP addresses, they navigate to domain names. This week you configure a real domain name for Edge Portfolio and set up HTTPS, which is now required (browsers mark HTTP sites as "Not Secure", Google penalises HTTP sites in search rankings, and many APIs refuse to work without HTTPS).

DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book. When a user types your domain into a browser, the DNS resolver looks up the IP address for that domain. You control this mapping by configuring records at your domain registrar or a DNS provider (Cloudflare is the standard, free tier, fast propagation, and useful additional features).

DNS record types you need: A record maps a domain to an IPv4 address (yourdomain.com → 1.2.3.4). AAAA maps to an IPv6 address. CNAME (Canonical Name) maps a domain to another domain name (www → yourdomain.com). MX records specify mail servers. TXT records contain arbitrary text, used for domain ownership verification, SPF/DKIM for email, and other security records.

TTL (Time to Live): how long DNS resolvers cache your record. A low TTL (60 seconds) means changes propagate quickly but every DNS lookup hits your authoritative server. A high TTL (86400, one day) means changes take a day to reach all users but DNS lookups are served from cache. Use low TTL when you are making changes; increase it after things are stable.

HTTPS via Let's Encrypt: Let's Encrypt is a free Certificate Authority. It issues SSL/TLS certificates that browsers trust. Certbot is the standard client, it authenticates your domain ownership (via a temporary file it places on your server, or via DNS), requests the certificate, installs it in nginx, and sets up automatic renewal. Certificates expire in 90 days. Certbot renews them automatically (via a cron job or systemd timer) before they expire.

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security): a response header that tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your domain, even if the user types http://. Once a browser has seen the HSTS header, it refuses HTTP connections to your domain for the specified duration.

items.title: Domains, registrars, and what you're actually buying
items.body:
## What it is
A domain name (yourname.com) is a human-readable address that points to your infrastructure. You don't own a domain forever, you lease it, usually yearly, from a registrar (Namecheap, Cloudflare, etc.) who is accredited to sell names under a TLD (.com, .dev, .io).

## Why it matters
Users navigate to names, not IP addresses or `random123.cloudfront.net` URLs. A custom domain is what makes Edge Portfolio feel like a real product instead of a demo. It is also the foundation everything else this week builds on, HTTPS certificates are issued for a domain, so you need the domain first.

## Choosing well
- Keep it short and spellable (someone will type it from a business card)
- `.com` is still the most trusted; `.dev` and `.io` are fine for engineers
- Budget ~$10-15/year. Beware $1 first-year deals that renew at $40

## Where this fits
Today you buy one real domain for Edge Portfolio. Every remaining day this week, DNS, the TLS certificate, the HTTPS redirect, attaches to this name.

items.title: DNS, nameservers, and pointing your domain at AWS Route 53
items.body:
## What it is
DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book: it translates a name (yourdomain.com) into the address of whatever should answer (here, your CloudFront distribution). The authoritative source for your domain's records is a set of nameservers.

Route 53 is AWS's DNS service. To let AWS answer for your domain, you:
1. Create a **hosted zone** for yourdomain.com in Route 53 → it gives you 4 nameservers
2. Go to your registrar and replace its default nameservers with those 4

From then on, the world asks Route 53 for your domain's records.

## Why it matters, propagation
Nameserver changes don't take effect instantly. Resolvers around the world cache the old answer until it expires. This propagation can take 5-60 minutes (sometimes longer). You verify it with `dig`:

```bash
dig NS yourdomain.com
# should list the 4 Route 53 nameservers
```

## Where this fits
Today you create the hosted zone and repoint your registrar's nameservers to Route 53. This is the switch that hands DNS control to AWS, so Terraform can manage your records next.

cards.prompt: DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the address of the server that should answer.
cards.whenRight: Right, it's the internet's phone book: name in, address out.
cards.whenWrong: That's DNS in one line: it maps yourdomain.com to wherever requests should go (e.g. CloudFront).
cards.sim:
dig yourdomain.com
# -> points to CloudFront

cards.prompt: Changing your domain's nameservers takes effect instantly worldwide.
cards.whenRight: Right, propagation takes 5-60 min as cached records expire across global resolvers.
cards.whenWrong: Nameserver changes propagate over minutes to an hour. Resolvers cache the old answer until its TTL expires.
cards.sim:
$ dig NS yourdomain.com
# wait until it lists the
# Route 53 nameservers

cards.prompt: A Route 53 hosted zone gives you nameservers that you then set at your domain registrar.
cards.whenRight: Exactly, create the zone, copy its 4 NS records to the registrar. That hands DNS to AWS.
cards.whenWrong: That's the flow: hosted zone -> 4 nameservers -> paste them at the registrar. Now AWS answers for your domain.

items.title: Route 53 hosted zone
items.body:
In AWS console → Route 53 → Hosted zones → Create hosted zone for yourdomain.com.
Note the 4 NS records.
Back in Namecheap → Domain List → Manage → Nameservers → 'Custom DNS' → paste the 4 NS records. Save.

Propagation takes 5-60 min. Check with: dig NS yourdomain.com

items.title: TLS certificates, Certificate Authorities, and AWS ACM
items.body:
## What it is
HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS encryption. For a browser to trust the encryption, your server presents a certificate signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) the browser already trusts. The cert proves 'this server really is yourdomain.com'.

ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) issues these certificates free and renews them automatically. You request a cert for yourdomain.com (and www.yourdomain.com), and ACM proves you own the domain via DNS validation, it asks you to add a special record (which it can auto-create in Route 53), then confirms it's there.

## Why it matters
- Browsers mark plain HTTP as 'Not Secure' and Google ranks it lower
- Auto-renewal means you never get paged at 2am for an expired cert (a classic outage)
- CloudFront requires the ACM cert to be in **us-east-1** specifically, a detail that trips up everyone once

## Where this fits
Today you request a free ACM certificate (in us-east-1!) for your domain, validated via DNS through the Route 53 zone you created yesterday. Tomorrow you attach it to CloudFront.

cards.prompt: A TLS certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority is what lets browsers show the padlock for HTTPS.
cards.whenRight: Right, the browser trusts the CA, the CA vouches for your domain, so the padlock appears.
cards.whenWrong: That's the chain of trust: CA signs your cert, browser trusts the CA, padlock shows. No trusted cert = no padlock.

cards.prompt: An ACM certificate used with CloudFront must be requested in the us-east-1 region.
cards.whenRight: Right, CloudFront only reads certs from us-east-1. Request it there even if everything else is elsewhere.
cards.whenWrong: CloudFront requires the cert in us-east-1, full stop. This catches everyone once, remember it.
cards.sim:
# ACM region for CloudFront:
# always us-east-1

cards.prompt: AWS ACM certificates are expensive and must be manually renewed every 90 days.
cards.whenRight: Right, ACM certs are free AND auto-renew. No 90-day scramble, no cost.
cards.whenWrong: ACM is free and renews automatically. The manual-90-day pain is Let's Encrypt-by-hand, not ACM.

 Click 'Create records in Route 53' → it auto-adds the validation records.

Wait 5-15 min for status to go to 'Issued'.

items.title: Wiring it together: aliases, viewer certs, and Route 53 alias records
items.body:
## What it is
Now you connect the three pieces in Terraform so your domain serves the site over HTTPS:

1. **`aliases`** on the CloudFront distribution, tells CloudFront 'I also answer to yourdomain.com and www.yourdomain.com'
2. **`viewer_certificate`** with your ACM cert ARN, replaces the default `*.cloudfront.net` cert so HTTPS works for YOUR name
3. A **Route 53 alias record**, an A record pointing your apex domain at the CloudFront distribution

## Why an ALIAS record, not a CNAME
The apex (yourdomain.com with no `www`) cannot be a CNAME, DNS forbids it. Route 53's alias record is an AWS-specific A record that points at an AWS resource (CloudFront) and resolves correctly at the apex. This is exactly the kind of edge case IaC documents for you so you never re-learn it.

## Why it matters
This day is where everything from the week becomes one coherent stack, all in `main.tf`, all version-controlled. Change the cert later? It's a diff. Move domains? It's a diff.

## Where this fits
Today you update `main.tf` with aliases, the viewer certificate, and the Route 53 alias record, then `terraform apply`. After propagation, your domain is wired to CloudFront over HTTPS.

cards.prompt: The CloudFront `aliases` setting tells the distribution which custom domain names it should answer to.
cards.whenRight: Right, without aliases, CloudFront only answers to its default *.cloudfront.net name.
cards.whenWrong: aliases is the list of custom domains CloudFront accepts. Omit it and your domain won't route to the distribution.

cards.prompt: You can use a CNAME record for the apex domain (yourdomain.com with no www).
cards.whenRight: Right, DNS forbids a CNAME at the apex. Use a Route 53 ALIAS record instead.
cards.whenWrong: The apex can't be a CNAME (DNS rule). Route 53's ALIAS record solves it, an A record that targets an AWS resource.
cards.sim:
# apex (yourdomain.com):
# CNAME -> not allowed
# ALIAS -> works (Route 53)

cards.prompt: Attaching your ACM certificate via `viewer_certificate` is what makes HTTPS work for your custom domain.
cards.whenRight: Exactly, it swaps the default cert for yours, so the padlock validates against your name.
cards.whenWrong: viewer_certificate points CloudFront at your ACM cert. Without it, HTTPS only works for *.cloudfront.net.

items.title: Update main.tf
Verifying HTTPS end-to-end and reading a certificate
items.body:
## What it is
Provisioning isn't done until you've verified it from the outside. After DNS + CloudFront propagate (10-15 min), you visit `https://yourdomain.com` and confirm:
- The page loads over HTTPS
- The browser shows a **padlock** (no 'Not Secure' warning)
- The certificate details show it was **issued by Amazon Trust Services** for your domain

## Why it matters, verify, don't assume
`terraform apply` succeeding means AWS accepted your config, not that the live experience works. DNS could still be propagating, the cert could be attached to the wrong domain, a redirect could be misconfigured. A senior engineer's habit is to check the actual user-facing result, every time, before calling it done.

Click the padlock → 'Connection is secure' → certificate. Reading a cert (who issued it, what names it covers, when it expires) is a core debugging skill you'll use whenever HTTPS misbehaves.

## Where this fits
Today is the verification gate for v0.2: your real domain, loading your portfolio, over a valid certificate. If the padlock is there and the cert names your domain, the HTTPS work is proven.

cards.prompt: A successful `terraform apply` guarantees the live site works for end users immediately.
cards.whenRight: Right, apply means AWS accepted the config. DNS/CloudFront may still propagate; always verify externally.
cards.whenWrong: apply only means the config was accepted. The user-facing result can still be propagating or misconfigured. Verify it.
cards.sim:
terraform apply # ok != live yet
# then: open https://yourdomain.com

cards.prompt: Clicking the browser padlock lets you inspect who issued the certificate and which domains it covers.
cards.whenRight: Right, padlock -> certificate details. Reading certs is a core HTTPS debugging skill.
cards.whenWrong: The padlock reveals the cert: issuer, covered names, expiry. Knowing how to read it is essential for debugging HTTPS.

cards.prompt: An ACM-issued certificate will show as issued by 'Amazon Trust Services' in the browser.
cards.whenRight: Right, that's ACM's CA. Seeing it confirms your cert is the ACM one you provisioned.
cards.whenWrong: ACM certs chain to Amazon Trust Services. Seeing that issuer confirms the right cert is attached.

Browser shows the padlock. Check the cert details, issued by Amazon Trust Services.

items.title: Security headers and HSTS: hardening the response
items.body:
## What it is
HTTPS encrypts the connection, but you can harden the site further with response headers that instruct the browser to behave safely. The key ones:

```text
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 # HSTS, always use HTTPS
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff # don't guess content types
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
```

HSTS is the important one: once a browser sees it, it refuses to connect to your domain over plain HTTP for the duration, even if the user types `http://`. It closes the brief window where a first HTTP request could be intercepted and downgraded.

## Why it matters
These headers are free, set-once, and meaningfully raise your security posture. Tools like securityheaders.com grade your site A-to-F based on which headers you send, and recruiters and security reviewers do check. CloudFront applies them via a response headers policy, declared in Terraform like everything else.

## Where this fits
Today you add a CloudFront response headers policy setting HSTS + the hardening headers, apply it, and confirm an A grade on securityheaders.com. That grade is a concrete, linkable proof of competence on the portfolio.

cards.prompt: HSTS tells the browser to always use HTTPS for your domain, even if the user types http://.
cards.whenRight: Right, once seen, the browser refuses plain HTTP to your domain for the max-age duration.
cards.whenWrong: That's HSTS: after the first time, the browser auto-upgrades and refuses HTTP. Closes the downgrade window.
cards.sim:
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
# browser: HTTPS only, no exceptions

cards.prompt: Security headers like HSTS and X-Content-Type-Options require buying an extra AWS service.
cards.whenRight: Right, they're free response headers, set via a CloudFront response headers policy in Terraform.
cards.whenWrong: They're free, just headers CloudFront adds. No extra service, declared in your existing main.tf.

cards.prompt: securityheaders.com grades a site based on which security response headers it sends.
cards.whenRight: Right, it's a quick external grade (A-F). Aiming for A is a concrete, linkable portfolio proof.
cards.whenWrong: It scans your response headers and grades A-F. Add HSTS + the hardening headers and you reach grade A.

items.title: Response headers policy
items.body:
Add a CloudFront response headers policy in Terraform that sets:
 Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
 Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

Verify with securityheaders.com, aim for grade A.

items.title: Acceptance criteria and tagging a release
items.body:
## What it is
A version ships when it meets its acceptance criteria, an explicit checklist of what 'done' means, not when you feel finished. For Edge Portfolio v0.2:

```text
[ ] https://yourdomain.com loads
[ ] www redirects to apex (or both work)
[ ] ACM certificate is valid
[ ] securityheaders.com grade A or better
[ ] v0.2 tag pushed
```

Then you tag the release in git:

```bash
git commit -m 'v0.2: custom domain + HTTPS + security headers'
git tag v0.2 && git push --tags
```

## Why it matters
A git tag is an immutable marker of a known-good state. `v0.1` was the bare CloudFront URL; `v0.2` is your hardened custom domain. Tags let you (and anyone reading the repo) see the project's progression and check out any past version exactly as it shipped. A checklist + tag is how professionals close a unit of work, no ambiguity about what was delivered.

## Where this fits
Today you run the acceptance checklist, fix anything that fails, and tag v0.2. Edge Portfolio now lives at your own domain, over HTTPS, with an A security grade and a clean version history.

cards.prompt: Acceptance criteria are an explicit checklist defining 'done' before you call a version shipped.
cards.whenRight: Right, done is a checklist you can verify, not a feeling. Every item must pass.
cards.whenWrong: Acceptance criteria make 'done' objective. You ship when every box is checked, not when you're tired of it.

cards.prompt: A git tag like `v0.2` is an immutable marker you can use to check out exactly that shipped state later.
cards.whenRight: Right, tags pin a known-good commit. `git checkout v0.2` restores precisely what shipped.
cards.whenWrong: Tags are permanent pointers to a commit. They let you (and reviewers) revisit any released version exactly.
cards.sim:

weeks.project: Edge Portfolio v0.2, live on YOUR domain with HTTPS, HSTS, and grade-A security headers, all in Terraform.
exercises: Add a wildcard cert (*.yourdomain.com) and create a sub-domain (blog.yourdomain.com)
Add IPv6 support to CloudFront
Add a 301 redirect rule from non-www to www (or vice versa)
questions: Why must ACM certs for CloudFront live in us-east-1 specifically?
What's an apex/zone-apex record?
What does HSTS preload mean?
What happens if your domain expires?
mastery_questions: You run certbot --nginx -d yourdomain.com and get "Error: Failed to connect to host for DVSNI challenge." What is happening? Certbot's ACME HTTP-01 challenge works by: Certbot places a file at /.well-known/acme-challenge/[token] on your server. Let's Encrypt's servers make an HTTP request to http://yourdomain.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/[token]. If it matches, the domain is verified. This fails when: your A record does not point to this server (DNS not propagated, or pointing to the wrong IP), port 80 is blocked by ufw, or nginx is not running. Check each in order: dig yourdomain.com A, ufw status, systemctl status nginx.

Your Let's Encrypt certificate expires in 3 days. Certbot's automatic renewal has not worked. How do you manually renew it? Run: sudo certbot renew --force-renewal. This forces renewal even though the certificate is not yet within the usual 30-day renewal window. If it fails, check: does Certbot still have a working configuration file at /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/yourdomain.com.conf? Is port 80 open (required for the HTTP-01 challenge)? Has nginx configuration changed since the original certificate was issued? The renewal log is at /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log.

What is the difference between a wildcard certificate and a single-domain certificate? A single-domain certificate is valid for one hostname (yourdomain.com) and optionally a second (www.yourdomain.com if you include both with -d). A wildcard certificate (*.yourdomain.com) is valid for any subdomain of yourdomain.com, api.yourdomain.com, blog.yourdomain.com, anything.yourdomain.com. Wildcard certificates require DNS-01 validation (proving domain ownership via a TXT record in DNS) instead of HTTP-01, because the challenge must be independent of the web server (there is no specific server to place a file on for "every subdomain"). Let's Encrypt supports wildcard certificates via the DNS-01 challenge.

Explain what HSTS preloading is and what the risk of setting it up incorrectly is. HSTS tells browsers "always use HTTPS for this domain." HSTS preloading takes it further, major browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) maintain a hardcoded list of domains that always require HTTPS, regardless of whether the browser has previously visited the site. If your domain is on the preload list, it is enforced even on first visit. The risk: if you ever need to downgrade to HTTP (your HTTPS is broken, your certificate is invalid), HSTS-preloaded domains will be inaccessible in every browser until the preloading is removed, which takes months (the browser update cycle). Only preload if you are certain HTTPS is permanent.
ai_assist: "Write the complete nginx configuration for a Node.js app with: HTTP to HTTPS redirect, HTTPS with Let's Encrypt certificate at /etc/letsencrypt/live/yourdomain.com/, proxy to localhost:3000, HSTS header with 1 year max-age, security headers (X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy), and gzip compression."

"Write a Cloudflare DNS configuration for: apex domain pointing to server IP (A record), www subdomain as CNAME to apex, and mail server MX record pointing to mail.yourdomain.com. Also explain which records should have Cloudflare proxying enabled and which should be DNS-only."

"Explain the ACME protocol that Let's Encrypt uses. Walk through the HTTP-01 challenge step by step: what Certbot sends, what Let's Encrypt verifies, what token is used, and how the certificate is issued."
weeks.pre_flight: Buy a domain name (Namecheap or Cloudflare Registrar). Set the nameservers to Cloudflare's (if using Cloudflare DNS). Create an A record pointing your domain to your server IP. Wait for DNS propagation (check with: dig yourdomain.com A). Install Certbot: sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx. Make sure your domain resolves to your server before running certbot, it needs to make an HTTP request to your server for domain validation.
common_mistakes: Running certbot before DNS has propagated. Let's Encrypt's servers must be able to reach your server via the domain name. If the A record is not pointing to your server yet, the challenge fails. Use dig and external DNS checkers to verify before running certbot.

Not setting up automatic certificate renewal. Let's Encrypt certificates expire in 90 days. Certbot installs a cron job or systemd timer for renewal automatically, but verify it is working: sudo certbot renew --dry-run. A certificate that expires is an outage.

Using self-signed certificates in production. Self-signed certificates are not trusted by browsers, users see a security warning. They are fine for internal development. In production, use Let's Encrypt.

Not redirecting HTTP to HTTPS. If your site serves both HTTP and HTTPS, Google indexes both, creating duplicate content issues. Users on HTTP never get the security benefits of HTTPS. Set up a permanent redirect (301) from HTTP to HTTPS in nginx.

Setting an overly long HSTS max-age on a site that is not ready. If HSTS is set to one year and you have a certificate issue, users are locked out for a year. Start with max-age=300 (5 minutes) while testing, then increase to 31536000 (one year) once confident.
weeks.debug_help: Certificate not trusted by browser (shows "Not Secure" even with HTTPS): check that Let's Encrypt issued the certificate (not a self-signed one). Run: openssl s_client -connect yourdomain.com:443 and check the issuer. Mixed content warnings: your page loads over HTTPS but some resources (images, scripts) are loaded over HTTP. Find them in Chrome DevTools > Console (mixed content errors) and update the URLs to HTTPS. nginx HTTPS config not working after certbot: certbot modifies nginx config automatically. Check /etc/nginx/sites-available/default for the SSL configuration it added. If you have a custom nginx config file, certbot may have modified the wrong file. Domain resolves but times out: your ufw firewall may be blocking port 443. Run: sudo ufw allow 443 and then test again.
stretch: Set up Cloudflare in front of your server. Change your A record to Cloudflare's proxy mode (the orange cloud). Cloudflare now sits between your users and your server, it provides DDoS protection, CDN caching for static assets, and hides your server's real IP. Configure Cloudflare's SSL mode to "Full (strict)" to require a valid certificate between Cloudflare and your server.

Configure automated SSL certificate monitoring. Write a script (or use a service like SSL Labs' API) that checks your certificate expiry date weekly and sends a notification if it is less than 30 days away. This is a redundant layer on top of Certbot's auto-renewal.

Implement Certificate Transparency monitoring. CT logs record every certificate issued for your domain. Set up an alert (via Facebook's Cert Transparency Monitoring, or crt.sh) that notifies you when any certificate is issued for your domain. This catches certificate mis-issuance or phishing attempts.

The same region as your S3 bucket

weeks.title: Edge Portfolio v0.3: GitHub Actions CI/CD
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment is the practice that makes software teams move fast without breaking things. Before CI/CD: a developer writes code, tests it locally (maybe), and manually deploys to the server (SSH in, git pull, restart service, hope nothing broke). After CI/CD: every push to the repository automatically runs tests and (if they pass) deploys to the server. The human is removed from the deployment process. This sounds scary; it is actually what makes deployment less scary.

GitHub Actions is the CI/CD system built into GitHub. Every repository gets free minutes for public repos and a monthly quota for private repos. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/ that define what happens when events occur (push to main, pull request opened, manual trigger). Each workflow runs on a virtual machine provided by GitHub (the runner). You choose the runner OS: ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest.

The deployment step: after the code passes tests, you need to get the new code onto your server. Several approaches. Direct SSH deploy: the GitHub Action SSHs into your server, pulls the latest code, and restarts the service (simple, works for a single server). Container-based deploy: build a Docker image, push to a container registry, SSH into the server and pull the new image (more complex, but the image is tested and immutable). For now, direct SSH is fine.

Secrets management in GitHub Actions: never hardcode server credentials in your workflow file. Use repository secrets: Settings > Secrets and Variables > Actions > New Repository Secret. In the workflow, reference them as ${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}. These are encrypted and only exposed to workflows, GitHub employees cannot read them.

Deployment safety: a deploy script that runs git pull && npm install && npm run build && systemctl restart app has a window where the service is stopped and new code is not yet running. For a personal portfolio, this is acceptable (seconds of downtime). For production services, use zero-downtime deployment strategies: blue-green deployment, rolling updates, or at minimum: build first, then swap.

concept_check.q: Why does CI/CD make deploys LESS scary, not more?
choices: Removing the human from `ssh prod && git pull && restart` removes the most common deploy failure: typos and forgotten steps. The pipeline runs identically every time, and you see green/red BEFORE traffic reaches the change
concept_check.explain: The pre-CI/CD deploy script lived in someone's head. They'd SSH in, pull, install, restart. Half the time they'd forget a step. CI/CD codifies the steps as YAML; the runner executes them identically every time. Plus tests run BEFORE deploy, broken commits never reach the server. The scary part of deploys is the variability; CI/CD removes it.

concept_check.q: Why do GitHub Actions runners get fresh state on every workflow run?
choices: Hermetic builds, no state leaks between runs, so a passing build on your laptop and on CI mean the same thing. Caching is opt-in and explicit, not a side effect
concept_check.explain: If runners reused state, a green CI build could mean 'the cached node_modules from last week happens to work'. Fresh runners force the workflow to install everything from scratch every time, so when CI passes, you know that exact `package-lock.json` actually builds. Caching is added back through `actions/cache` with explicit keys, never implicit.

concept_check.q: Why do you store secrets in GitHub's `Secrets` UI and not in the workflow YAML?
choices: Secrets in the YAML get committed to the repo, end up in git history, leak via PRs, get scraped by bots. GitHub's encrypted Secrets are exposed to the workflow as env vars at runtime without touching disk
concept_check.explain: The classic mistake: hardcoding `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA...` in the workflow YAML. That commit is now permanent, even if you rotate the key, anyone with repo history can see what you used. GitHub Secrets are encrypted at rest, decrypted into env vars only inside the runner, and never appear in logs (GitHub masks them). Use them from day one.

days.title: What is CI/CD?
days.summary: The discipline that removes the human from deploy.

items.title: Before and after CI/CD
items.body:
## Before
A developer writes code. Tests it locally (maybe). SSHs into the server. `git pull && npm install && npm run build && systemctl restart app`. Hopes nothing broke. If it broke, SSHs back in, debugs at 2am.

## After
A developer writes code. Pushes to GitHub. A workflow runs: install deps → run tests → build → deploy. If tests fail, deploy doesn't happen, the developer sees the red ❌ in PR. If they pass, the server gets the new code automatically.

The human is REMOVED from the deploy path. That's the whole point.

## CI vs CD, the two halves
```text
CI (Continuous Integration)
 Every push: pull, install, lint, test, build.
 Verdict: green or red. Visible on the PR.
 Goal: catch breakage BEFORE merge.

CD (Continuous Deployment / Delivery)
 Every merge to main: deploy the green build to production.
 Goal: main is always shippable; deploy is a non-event.
```

## What GitHub Actions gives you
- A YAML file in `.github/workflows/` defines the workflow.
- Workflows trigger on events: `push`, `pull_request`, `workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`.
- Each run gets a fresh Ubuntu/macOS/Windows VM (the runner).
- Free minutes: 2,000/month for private repos, unlimited for public.

## What you build this week
`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` that runs on every push to `main`:
1. Checks out the repo
2. Validates the HTML (a basic test)
3. Configures AWS credentials from GitHub Secrets
4. Syncs `index.html` to S3
5. Invalidates CloudFront so the new file goes live

You'll push a change to `index.html` and watch it land on your live URL ~90 seconds later. No SSH, no typing, no fear.

cards.prompt: CI means deploying to production on every push.
cards.whenRight: Right, CI = Continuous Integration (build + test on every push). CD = the deploy half. Different concepts that team up.
cards.whenWrong: CI is the build/test half. CD is the deploy half. Together: CI/CD. Distinct concepts.

cards.prompt: GitHub Actions workflows live as YAML files in `.github/workflows/`.
cards.whenRight: Right, convention is hard-coded. Folder, filename, schema all defined by GitHub.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, `.github/workflows/<name>.yml`. Standard location; one file per workflow.

cards.prompt: Removing the human from deploys makes deploys MORE risky.
cards.whenRight: Right, opposite. Humans typo and forget steps; pipelines run identically every time. Removing the human reduces variance.
cards.whenWrong: Less risky. The human IS the variance. Pipelines = consistency = boring deploys, which is the goal.

days.title: AWS IAM user for CI
days.summary: A least-privileged user the workflow can sign requests with.

items.title: Why a dedicated IAM user for CI
items.body:
## The principle of least privilege
The IAM user your workflow uses should be able to do ONLY what the workflow needs and nothing else. If a credential leaks, the blast radius is exactly the workflow's permissions.

## What the workflow needs
1. PUT objects into your S3 bucket (sync `index.html`).
2. Invalidate CloudFront for the matching distribution.

That's it. No EC2, no IAM, no Route53, no SSM, none of which the workflow touches.

## Create the user (AWS console)
1. **IAM → Users → Create user**.
2. Name: `edge-portfolio-ci`.
3. **DO NOT** enable AWS Management Console access. Programmatic access only.
4. Skip groups → Next → Create user.
5. After creation: open the user → **Security credentials → Create access key** → **Application running outside AWS**.
6. Download the CSV with `Access key ID` + `Secret access key`. **You will see the secret ONCE.**

## Attach the minimal policy
User → Permissions → Add permissions → Attach policies directly → Create policy → JSON tab. Paste (replace YOUR-BUCKET + YOUR-DIST):

```json
{
 "Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [
 {
 "Sid": "S3SyncSiteOnly",
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
 "Resource": [
 "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET",
 "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET/*"
 ]
 },
 {
 "Sid": "InvalidateCloudFront",
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": ["cloudfront:CreateInvalidation"],
 "Resource": "arn:aws:cloudfront::*:distribution/YOUR-DIST"
 }
 ]
}
```

Save as `EdgePortfolioCiPolicy`. Attach to the user. Done.

## The rule for every CI credential going forward
- Dedicated IAM user per pipeline (never reuse your dev creds).
- Programmatic access only (no console login).
- Inline policy that names the exact resources, never `*`.
- Rotate the access key every 90 days.

This is the practice that prevents the disasters.

cards.prompt: Reusing your personal AWS access key for CI is a fine shortcut for a personal project.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Your dev key has broad permissions; a leak via CI logs = everything compromised. Dedicated CI user = scoped blast radius.
cards.whenWrong: Wrong. Dedicated CI user, minimal policy, rotatable independently. Same effort for huge safety upgrade.

cards.prompt: An IAM policy with `"Resource": "*"` is the safe default.
cards.whenRight: Right, opposite. `*` means every resource. Scope to the exact bucket ARN + the exact distribution ID.
cards.whenWrong: `*` is the dangerous default. Always name the specific resource ARNs. Tedious; necessary.

cards.prompt: The secret access key is shown to you ONCE on creation; lose it and you must create a new one.
cards.whenRight: Right, same pattern as OpenAI / GitHub keys. Show-once is industry-wide.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, once. Save it carefully (or just rotate and replace). AWS never shows it again.

2. Create the inline policy from the lesson (substitute YOUR bucket name + distribution ID).
3. Attach to the user. Generate access key.
4. Save the Access Key ID + Secret in a password manager (NOT in the repo).
5. In `cicd/IAM.md`: paste the policy + note the user's ARN.

days.title: Add secrets to GitHub
days.summary: Where the AWS keys live, encrypted, scoped to the repo.

items.title: Secrets, not env vars in YAML
items.body:
## The mechanism
GitHub Repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret.

Add three:
```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (from step 2)
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (from step 2)
CLOUDFRONT_DISTRIBUTION_ID (the distribution ID, e.g. E1A2B3C4D5E6F7)
```

At workflow runtime they're available as:
```yaml
env:
 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
```

## What GitHub does for you
- Encrypted at rest (libsodium sealed boxes).
- Only available inside workflow runs of THIS repo (not even forks of public repos can read them).
- Automatically masked in workflow logs, if a step accidentally prints `$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, GitHub replaces it with `***`.
- Rotation is a single UI action.

## What you must still do
- Don't echo secrets explicitly via `set -x` or `env | grep AWS`. Masking helps but isn't perfect.
- Don't pass secrets to `if` conditions in YAML, the entire expression can leak in logs.
- Rotate the AWS key (and update both GitHub Secrets) every 90 days.

## Environment secrets (for later)
GitHub also supports per-environment secrets (`production` vs `staging`) and protection rules (require manual approval for prod deploys). For Edge Portfolio v0.3 you only have prod, repo-level secrets are enough.

cards.prompt: GitHub masks secrets in workflow logs by replacing them with `***`.
cards.whenRight: Right, automatic masking. Useful safety net; not a substitute for not echoing secrets in the first place.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, `***`. Backup defence. Don't rely on it alone; structure your YAML so secrets never appear in command output.

cards.prompt: Forks of a public repo can read its repository secrets.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Secrets are scoped to the upstream repo. PRs from forks run with restricted permissions and no secrets.
cards.whenWrong: Forks can't. This is critical, it's why PR workflows from forks can't deploy. Plan accordingly.

cards.prompt: Per-environment secrets + protection rules are necessary even for a personal portfolio with only one environment.
cards.whenRight: Right, repo-level secrets are fine for one environment. Per-env + manual approval matter when prod and staging coexist.
cards.whenWrong: Overkill for one env. Repo secrets here; per-env later when staging exists.

2. Add AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY + CLOUDFRONT_DISTRIBUTION_ID.
3. Confirm they appear in the list (values hidden).
4. NOTES.md: list the secrets you added and where to rotate them.

days.title: Write the workflow
days.summary: .github/workflows/deploy.yml, the whole pipeline.

items.title: The deploy workflow
items.body:
## File location
`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, GitHub auto-discovers anything in this folder.

## The complete workflow
```yaml
name: Deploy to S3 + invalidate CloudFront

on:
 push:
 branches: [main] # only on main
 workflow_dispatch: # plus manual trigger for testing

jobs:
 deploy:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - name: Checkout
 uses: actions/checkout@v4

 - name: Configure AWS credentials
 uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
 with:
 aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
 aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
 aws-region: us-east-1

 - name: Sync site to S3
 run: |
 aws s3 sync . s3://YOUR-BUCKET-NAME \
 --exclude '.git/*' \
 --exclude '.github/*' \
 --exclude '*.md' \
 --delete

 - name: Invalidate CloudFront
 run: |
 aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
 --distribution-id ${{ secrets.CLOUDFRONT_DISTRIBUTION_ID }} \
 --paths '/*'
```

## Read it line by line
- `on.push.branches: [main]`, runs ONLY when main updates. PR pushes don't trigger deploy.
- `workflow_dispatch`, gives you a "Run workflow" button in the Actions tab.
- `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, fresh Ubuntu VM, no leftover state.
- `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4`, official AWS action. Pin to a version, not `@main`.
- `aws s3 sync ... --delete`, uploads changed files, removes files from the bucket that aren't in the repo. Aggressive but accurate.
- `--exclude` patterns keep `.git/`, workflows, and READMEs out of the bucket.
- The invalidation has cost: $0.005/path beyond the free 1,000/month per account. `/*` invalidates everything; cheap.

## Commit and watch
```bash
git add .github/workflows/deploy.yml
git commit -m 'ci: add S3 + CloudFront deploy workflow'
git push origin main
```
Open https://github.com/YOU/edge-portfolio/actions, there will be a run in progress (or failed, fix and re-push). Click into it to see each step's output.

cards.prompt: `@v4` on the official AWS action is safer than `@main`.
cards.whenRight: Right, version pin = predictable behaviour. `@main` lets the action change under you silently.
cards.whenWrong: Pin versions. `@main` makes your pipeline depend on someone else's HEAD. Pin to a tag; upgrade deliberately.

cards.prompt: `aws s3 sync --delete` is destructive and can remove files you didn't intend.
cards.whenRight: Right, anything in the bucket not in your repo gets DELETED. Test in a non-prod bucket first.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, destructive. Excellent for keeping bucket = repo, but verify the `--exclude` patterns; one wrong glob and you wipe the wrong file.

cards.prompt: CloudFront invalidations are free.
cards.whenRight: Right, 1,000/month free per account, then $0.005/path. Use `/*` for full invalidation; very cheap unless you're inval'ing thousands of paths/day.
cards.whenWrong: Has a free tier then per-path cost. For a portfolio, the cost is irrelevant; for a CMS-driven site, design the invalidation strategy carefully.

days.title: Test the pipeline
days.summary: End-to-end: edit a file, push, watch it land on the live URL.

items.title: The test
items.body:
## The change
Edit `index.html`. Add an obvious visible change, a new sentence, a different background colour, anything you'll spot.

## The push
```bash
git add index.html
git commit -m 'test: visible change to confirm CI/CD pipeline'
git push origin main
```

## The watch
1. Open https://github.com/YOU/edge-portfolio/actions, see the run start.
2. Click into it. Each step expands to show output.
3. The `Sync site to S3` step should show `upload: index.html to s3://...`.
4. The `Invalidate CloudFront` step should print an Invalidation ID.
5. Total run time: ~30-60 seconds.

## The verify
1. Open your live URL (`https://yourdomain.com`).
2. **Hard refresh** (Ctrl+Shift+R or Cmd+Shift+R) to bypass browser cache.
3. The change is live.

## Common failures and what they actually mean
```text
 ❌ 'Unable to locate credentials'
 → secret name typo in YAML or secret not added in GitHub Settings.

 ❌ 'AccessDenied' on s3 PutObject
 → IAM policy missing the resource ARN or wrong bucket name.

 ❌ 'NoSuchBucket'
 → bucket name typo in YAML.

 ❌ 'AccessDenied' on cloudfront:CreateInvalidation
 → distribution ID wrong in secret OR IAM policy missing the dist ARN.

 ✓ Run green but site doesn't change
 → browser cache. Hard refresh; if still wrong, check CloudFront
 invalidation finished (Console → Distributions → Invalidations).
```

Read errors carefully, they almost always tell you exactly which step + which permission + which resource.

cards.prompt: A green CI run guarantees the change is live in the browser within seconds.
cards.whenRight: Right, CloudFront invalidations take 1-5 minutes to propagate edge-wide. AND the browser may show its own cached copy.
cards.whenWrong: Two cache layers: CloudFront edges (mins to invalidate) + browser. Hard refresh + wait.

cards.prompt: Reading the AWS error message in the failed step is the fastest debugging path.
cards.whenRight: Right, AWS errors are specific: which API, which resource, which permission. Read them.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, AWS errors are unusually informative. The step that failed names the API call; the API call names the resource; the resource names the permission.

cards.prompt: If the workflow is wrong, you should ALWAYS revert the deploy step first to prevent further damage.
cards.whenRight: Right, depends. CI/CD pipelines are forward-only by design. Fix the workflow YAML, push, run again. Reverting code is for code bugs, not pipeline bugs.
cards.whenWrong: Fix forward, don't revert. Pipeline failures don't pollute the bucket; the next push fixes things.

items.title: Your turn, end-to-end
items.body:
[CODE]
1. Edit index.html with a visible change.
2. Commit + push.
3. Watch the Actions tab; confirm green.
4. Hard refresh your live URL; confirm the change.
5. NOTES.md: record total time from `git push` to visible change.

days.title: Add an HTML validation step
days.summary: A real test that runs BEFORE deploy.

items.title: htmlhint as a gate
items.body: ## What you add A linting step that runs BEFORE the deploy step. If your HTML has errors, the workflow fails and deploy doesn't happen. ```yaml - name: Install htmlhint run: npm install -g htmlhint - name: Lint HTML run: htmlhint index.html ``` Place these between the `Configure AWS credentials` step and the `Sync site to S3` step. If `htmlhint` finds errors (unclosed tags, bad attributes, missing alt text), it exits non-zero and the workflow stops before any S3 write. ## htmlhint config, optional but recommended Add `.htmlhintrc` at the repo root: ```json { "doctype-first": true, "title-require": true, "tag-pair": true, "attr-no-duplication": true, "alt-require": true, "src-not-empty": true } ``` Now the gate is: `` present, doctype declared, tags balanced, `<img>` has `alt`, etc. The baseline a portfolio site should always meet. ## Test the gate Deliberately break index.html (remove `</body>`). Commit + push. Watch the workflow FAIL at the Lint HTML step. Deploy never runs. Fix the tag, push again, deploy runs. ## Why test gates matter This is the whole CI philosophy in miniature. The pipeline catches breakage BEFORE it hits prod. As you add more checks (link check, Lighthouse score, image size budget), each one becomes a gate. You ship faster because the pipeline guards quality.

cards.prompt: A failed lint step should still allow the deploy to proceed.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. The whole point of the gate is to STOP the deploy. A failed test = no deploy.
cards.whenWrong: No deploy if tests fail. That's the gate. If you bypass, the gate is decoration.

cards.prompt: Linting catches every HTML bug; you don't need to test in a browser anymore.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Lint catches structural issues. Browser testing catches rendering, interactivity, accessibility. Both layers.
cards.whenWrong: Different bugs. Linters: structure. Browsers: render. Both layers; neither replaces the other.

cards.prompt: Adding more gates (link check, Lighthouse, etc.) slows you down.
cards.whenRight: Right, opposite. Each gate catches a class of bug pre-deploy. Faster to fix in CI than to revert prod.
cards.whenWrong: Each gate REMOVES a class of regression. Gates compound; they don't slow you down once they're in place.

4. Fix the HTML. Push. Confirm workflow goes green + deploys.
5. Commit final state.

weeks.title: Edge Portfolio v0.4: Monitoring + logs
weeks.context:
You cannot improve what you cannot measure. Monitoring is the practice of collecting data about your system's health and setting up alerts so you know when something is wrong before your users do. In W1-W3, you built and deployed Edge Portfolio. In W4, you instrument it.

There are two types of monitoring. Black-box monitoring (also called synthetic monitoring or uptime monitoring) tests your system from the outside: an external service pings your URL every minute and alerts you if it does not get a 200 response. This is the first layer. It tells you the system is broken but not why.

White-box monitoring (also called telemetry) collects data from inside the system: the application exposes metrics (request count, error rate, latency), the server exposes system metrics (CPU, memory, disk), and you send logs to a centralised log management service. This tells you why the system is broken.

The four golden signals of service health (from Google's SRE book): Latency (how long does a request take?), Traffic (how many requests per second?), Errors (what rate of requests fail?), and Saturation (how full is the system, CPU, memory, disk?). An anomaly in any of these signals indicates a problem.

Structured logging: logs should be machine-parseable JSON, not free-text sentences. timestamp, level, message, requestId, userId, durationMs, statusCode as JSON fields allow you to query by any dimension. A free-text log ("Error: something went wrong for user 123") is useful when you are reading it; a structured log is useful when you are searching across millions of lines.

Uptime monitoring services: BetterUptime, UptimeRobot (free tier), Freshping. These send a request to your site every minute from multiple geographic locations and alert you (Slack, email, PagerDuty) if the response takes too long or is not 200. Your on-call starts with an uptime alert.

This week you set up uptime monitoring for Edge Portfolio, ship structured logging, and build a basic health check endpoint.

concept_check.q: Why is uptime monitoring (black-box) the first layer to add, not the deepest?
choices: Uptime probes test the system the way a USER does: hit the URL, did it respond? It catches the largest class of outages (the site is down) for the smallest setup cost. White-box telemetry comes second
concept_check.explain: Black-box monitoring asks the one question that matters most: from the outside, is the site up? It catches DNS failures, certificate issues, origin outages, edge problems, anything that breaks the user experience, without instrumentation inside your app. White-box (per-request logs, latency histograms, error rates per route) tells you WHY the site is down, but you start with black-box because it's 10 minutes to set up and catches the loudest failures.

concept_check.q: Why bother with a billing alarm even when your monthly bill is $1?
choices: Run-away costs from misconfiguration (recursive Lambda, infinite CloudFront invalidation loop, leaked key) escalate in hours, not weeks. A $50 alarm is the safety net that catches the bug before it becomes a $5,000 invoice
concept_check.explain: The horror stories are real: a developer's S3 key gets scraped from a public repo, the attacker spins up bitcoin miners, and the bill is $32,000 by morning. Or a Lambda that triggers itself spirals to $4,000 in 6 hours. A SNS-fed CloudWatch billing alarm at $50 catches these the moment the spend curve bends, while you still have time to act. Setup: 10 minutes. Insurance: priceless.

concept_check.q: Why is `5xx error rate` a more useful alarm than `total request count went down`?
choices: Drops in traffic could be legitimate (off-hours, weekend, marketing pause); a spike in 5xx is ALWAYS a real problem. The signal-to-noise ratio is dramatically better
concept_check.explain: Alarms should fire on signal, not noise. A traffic drop has a hundred legitimate causes (it's 3am, a marketing campaign ended, search ranked you lower this week). A 5xx spike has ~zero legitimate causes, it means requests are failing. The on-call discipline is to alarm on irreducible-signal metrics and rely on dashboards for the noisy ones.

days.title: Why monitor
days.summary: Black-box vs white-box; the four golden signals.

items.title: The two kinds of monitoring
items.body:
## Black-box (synthetic / uptime)
An external service hits your URL every minute from multiple regions. Did you respond 200 OK in under 5 seconds? If not, page someone.

```text
Probe (Tokyo) ──[GET https://yoursite.com]──> 200 OK in 280ms ✓
Probe (London) ──[GET https://yoursite.com]──> timeout ✗ ALERT
```

This is what users experience. If black-box says down, you're down.

## White-box (telemetry)
Your application emits metrics (CloudWatch / Prometheus / OTel) and logs about itself: request count, latency histogram, error rate per route, memory usage, queue depth.

This tells you WHY you're down. The black-box probe says "500s from London"; white-box logs say "the /api/users handler is timing out because the DB has 47% CPU".

## The four golden signals (Google SRE)
Per service, watch:
```text
1. LATENCY, how long does a request take?
2. TRAFFIC, how many requests per second?
3. ERRORS, what fraction fail?
4. SATURATION, how full is the system (CPU, memory, disk)?
```

Anomaly in any of those = the system is in trouble. If you only have time to watch four numbers, watch these.

## What you build this week
For Edge Portfolio (a static site, no app code), the monitoring stack is small:
1. Uptime ping every minute from BetterUptime / UptimeRobot.
2. CloudWatch billing alarm at $50 (cheap insurance).
3. CloudFront 5xx-error-rate alarm.
4. A tiny static status page reading from CloudWatch.

Total ops effort: ~3 hours. Outcome: you know within 60 seconds when the site goes down.

cards.whenRight: Right, Google SRE's irreducible four. Anomaly in any = real problem.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, LTES. Memorise these; they apply to any service.

cards.whenRight: Right, no. The billing alarm alone is worth 100x its setup cost. Uptime check is 5 minutes more.
