days.title: Uptime monitoring
days.summary: BetterUptime / UptimeRobot, set up the external probe.

items.title: Set up the probe
items.body:
## BetterUptime (recommended)
Free tier: 10 monitors, 3-minute checks, email + Slack alerts.

```text
1. Sign up at betterstack.com/better-uptime.
2. Monitors → Create monitor.
3. URL to monitor: https://yourdomain.com
4. Check frequency: 3 minutes (free) or 30 seconds (paid).
5. HTTP status code: 200 (default).
6. Alert when: HTTP code != 200 OR response time > 5 seconds.
7. Notification channels: email + Slack webhook (if you have one).
8. Save.
```

## UptimeRobot (alternative)
Free tier: 50 monitors, 5-minute checks, email alerts only.

## Test the alarm, important
You MUST verify the alarm fires before trusting it. Temporarily block your URL:
1. Edit your local hosts file: add `127.0.0.1 yourdomain.com` (so YOUR machine can't resolve it; the probe still can)., Actually this only tests YOUR machine; the probe is external.
2. Better test: in CloudFront, temporarily disable your distribution. Wait 2 minutes; the probe fails; you should get the alert email.
3. Re-enable the distribution. Probe recovers. You should get an 'Up' email.

## What 'good' looks like
```text
 ✓ You get the down alert email within 5 minutes of disabling.
 ✓ You get the up email within 5 minutes of re-enabling.
 ✓ Status page shows the incident in history.
```

If the alert doesn't fire, the monitor isn't useful. Test before relying on it.

## Public status page (optional)
BetterUptime generates a free public status page (status.betterstack.com/yourname). Link it from your portfolio's footer, recruiters love this signal.

cards.prompt: An untested uptime monitor is a placebo.
cards.whenRight: Right, never trust an alarm you haven't seen fire. Test deliberately.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, test it. Disable the origin, watch the alarm fire, re-enable. Now you trust the alarm.

cards.whenWrong: Yes, free tier suffices. The signal is the same; latency to detection differs.

days.title: Billing alarm
days.summary: The $50 alarm that prevents the $5,000 invoice.

items.title: CloudWatch billing alarm, required infrastructure
items.body:
## Why first
The single highest-leverage alarm you'll ever set up. 10 minutes; protects against the most expensive class of mistake: cost runaway.

## Manual setup (one-time)
AWS console (region us-east-1, billing metrics only exist there):
```text
1. Billing → Billing preferences → Receive Free Tier Usage Alerts + Billing Alerts → save.
 (Without this, no metrics flow to CloudWatch.)
2. CloudWatch (us-east-1) → Alarms → Create alarm.
3. Select metric → Billing → Total Estimated Charge → Currency: USD.
4. Threshold: Greater than $50.
5. Period: 6 hours (billing metrics update slowly).
6. Notification: New SNS topic → enter your email → confirm via the email link.
7. Name: BillingAlarm-50USD. Create.
```

## Terraform version (preferred, codify it)
```hcl
# billing-alarm.tf, apply once, sleep better forever
resource "aws_sns_topic" "billing_alerts" {
 name = "billing-alerts"
}

resource "aws_sns_topic_subscription" "billing_email" {
 topic_arn = aws_sns_topic.billing_alerts.arn
 protocol = "email"
 endpoint = "you@example.com"
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "billing_50usd" {
 provider = aws.useast1 # billing metrics ONLY in us-east-1
 alarm_name = "billing-50-usd"
 comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
 evaluation_periods = 1
 metric_name = "EstimatedCharges"
 namespace = "AWS/Billing"
 period = 21600 # 6 hours
 statistic = "Maximum"
 threshold = 50
 dimensions = { Currency = "USD" }
 alarm_actions = [aws_sns_topic.billing_alerts.arn]
}
```

After confirming the SNS subscription (email link), the alarm is active. It fires when CloudWatch's 6-hour estimate exceeds $50.

## Test it
You can manually transition the alarm state to test the notification path:
```bash
aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state \
 --alarm-name billing-50-usd \
 --state-value ALARM \
 --state-reason 'testing notification path' \
 --region us-east-1
```
You should get the email within seconds. Now you trust the alarm.

cards.prompt: Billing metrics are available in any AWS region.
cards.whenRight: Right, only us-east-1. CloudWatch billing alarms must be created there.
cards.whenWrong: us-east-1 only. AWS quirk. Document it; you'll forget otherwise.

cards.prompt: An SNS topic subscription requires email confirmation before notifications work.
cards.whenRight: Right, AWS sends a confirmation email; click the link or no alarms fire.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, click the confirm link. Untested subscriptions = silent alarms.

cards.prompt: A $50 threshold for a portfolio is too high, you'll never hit it.
cards.whenRight: Right, that's the POINT. The alarm catches the disaster scenario, not normal spend. $50 ≫ normal spend = clean signal.
cards.whenWrong: $50 = disaster threshold, not budget. Normal spend is $1-5; the alarm catches the runaway scenario.

days.title: 5xx error rate alarm
days.summary: Alarm on the signal that matters most for a CDN.

items.title: CloudFront 5xx alarm
items.body:
## Why this metric
For a CDN-fronted site, the four-signal mapping is:
- LATENCY → CloudWatch CloudFront `Latency` metric
- TRAFFIC → `Requests` metric
- ERRORS → `5xxErrorRate` (and `4xxErrorRate`)
- SATURATION → mostly N/A (CloudFront scales for you)

`5xxErrorRate` is the irreducible signal: percentage of requests that returned a 5xx. Spikes here = real problem.

## The alarm (Terraform)
```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "cloudfront_5xx" {
 provider = aws.useast1
 alarm_name = "cloudfront-5xx-rate-above-1pct"
 comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
 evaluation_periods = 2 # 2 consecutive periods
 metric_name = "5xxErrorRate"
 namespace = "AWS/CloudFront"
 period = 300 # 5-min buckets
 statistic = "Average"
 threshold = 1.0 # percent
 dimensions = {
 DistributionId = var.cloudfront_distribution_id
 Region = "Global"
 }
 alarm_actions = [aws_sns_topic.billing_alerts.arn]
 ok_actions = [aws_sns_topic.billing_alerts.arn] # notify on recovery too
 treat_missing_data = "notBreaching"
}
```

## Reading the parameters
- `threshold = 1.0`, fire when 5xx rate exceeds 1% of requests.
- `evaluation_periods = 2`, must be over threshold for TWO consecutive 5-min windows. Reduces flapping.
- `ok_actions`, notify on recovery too. Without this, you get the bad-news email and never the good-news email.
- `treat_missing_data = notBreaching`, if no data arrived (low traffic, weekend), don't fire.

## What the alarm catches
- Origin (S3) outage → CloudFront returns 5xx as a passthrough.
- Bucket policy misconfiguration → 403 disguised as 5xx in some cases.
- Lambda@Edge throwing (if you ever add one).
- Cert issues / TLS handshake failures.

## What it does NOT catch
- DNS pointing the wrong way (no requests = no 5xx data).
- Domain expired.
- Your phone is in airplane mode.
That's what the BetterUptime probe is for, different layer.

cards.prompt: `evaluation_periods = 2` reduces false alarms from one-off spikes.
cards.whenRight: Right, needs sustained breach, not a single noisy window. Classic anti-flapping pattern.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, sustained signal vs spike. 2 periods at 5min = ~10 mins of breach before fire.

cards.prompt: `ok_actions` notifies you when an alarm clears.
cards.whenRight: Right, without it you're left wondering if the incident self-resolved or you missed an alert.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, recovery is half the story. Always set ok_actions to the same SNS topic.

cards.prompt: An origin outage in S3 will show up as 5xx on CloudFront's metric.
cards.whenRight: Right, CloudFront passes the failure through. The 5xx rate jumps; your alarm fires.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, origin failures bubble up. The CDN is opinionated about masking some failures but 5xx generally surfaces.

items.title: CloudFront access logs
items.body:
## What they are
CloudFront can write a log entry to S3 for every request. Each entry: timestamp, edge location, client IP, request path, status code, bytes served, latency, referer, user agent.

## Why bother for a portfolio
- Real data to query (great practice for SQL on Athena later in the track).
- Detect anomalies (sudden 4xx spike, scraper hitting you).
- Trend analysis (when do recruiters actually visit your site?).

## Enable
```text
CloudFront console → Your distribution → Logs and metrics → Standard logging → Edit.
 Status: On
 S3 bucket: create new bucket cloudfront-logs-YOUR-NAME (us-east-1)
 Prefix: portfolio/
 Save.
```

## Or in Terraform
```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "cf_logs" {
 bucket = "cloudfront-logs-${var.yourname}"
}

resource "aws_cloudfront_distribution" "main" {
 # ... existing config ...
 logging_config {
 bucket = "${aws_s3_bucket.cf_logs.bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com"
 prefix = "portfolio/"
 include_cookies = false
 }
}
```

## Query with Athena (15-min setup)
1. Athena → Query editor → New query.
2. Create external table pointing at your logs bucket:
```sql
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE cf_logs (
 date_col DATE,
 time_col STRING,
 x_edge_loc STRING,
 sc_bytes BIGINT,
 c_ip STRING,
 cs_method STRING,
 cs_host STRING,
 cs_uri_stem STRING,
 sc_status INT,
 cs_referer STRING,
 cs_user_agent STRING
 -- ... cloudfront log format has more fields; abbreviated here
)
ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'
LOCATION 's3://cloudfront-logs-YOUR-NAME/portfolio/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('skip.header.line.count'='2');
```
3. Query:
```sql
-- 5xx rate by hour over last 7 days
SELECT
 date_trunc('hour', from_iso8601_timestamp(concat(cast(date_col as varchar), 'T', time_col))) AS hour,
 count(*) AS requests,
 sum(CASE WHEN sc_status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / count(*) AS error_rate_pct
FROM cf_logs
WHERE date_col > current_date - interval '7' day
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 DESC;
```

## Cost reality
- Logs in S3: ~$0.023 / GB-month. A portfolio generates KB/day. Effectively free.
- Athena queries: $5/TB scanned. Per query on logs: pennies.

Genuine portfolio data + real Athena queries = strong signal.

cards.prompt: CloudFront access logs are appropriate for portfolio-scale traffic from a cost perspective.
cards.whenRight: Right, KB/day of logs; pennies of storage; pennies of Athena queries. Free for real.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, costs are negligible at portfolio scale. Don't over-think; turn them on.

cards.prompt: Querying logs via Athena requires a separate ETL pipeline.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Athena queries raw S3 files. Define the schema; run SQL. No ETL.
cards.whenWrong: Athena does it directly. Schema-on-read; no pipeline needed for log analysis.

weeks.title: Docker, Containers from First Principles
weeks.context:
Docker solves the "works on my machine" problem. Before Docker: your Node application runs on your macOS laptop (Node 20, specific npm packages, specific system libraries). On the Ubuntu 22.04 production server with Node 18, a different npm package version, and different system libraries, it behaves differently. Docker packages your application and all its dependencies (including the OS libraries) into an immutable image. The image runs identically on your laptop, on CI, and on production.

A container is a running instance of an image. An image is a template, the blueprint. A container is a running process using that blueprint. You can run multiple containers from the same image simultaneously (they share the image but each has its own file system layer and process namespace).

Namespaces and cgroups: Docker is not a virtual machine. It does not emulate hardware. It uses Linux kernel features. Namespaces isolate processes (a process inside a container sees only its own filesystem, network interface, and process tree). cgroups limit resources (this container gets at most 512MB RAM and 0.5 CPU cores). The container shares the host kernel, this is why Docker on macOS and Windows requires a Linux virtual machine underneath (Docker Desktop). The result is lighter and faster than a VM.

Dockerfile: the recipe for building an image. FROM declares the base image. COPY brings files from your build context into the image. RUN executes commands during the build. EXPOSE declares which port the container uses. CMD sets the default command when the container starts. Every Dockerfile instruction creates a new layer in the image. Layers are cached, if a layer has not changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached layer (fast builds). Order your instructions from least-changing to most-changing to maximise cache hits.

Multi-stage builds: two FROM instructions in one Dockerfile. The first stage builds the application (installs devDependencies, compiles TypeScript). The second stage copies only the compiled output from the first stage and installs only production dependencies. The final image does not contain the build tools, it is smaller and more secure.

concept_check.q: What's the precise difference between a Docker image and a container?
choices: An image is an immutable blueprint (layers of files + metadata). A container is a running process started from an image. One image, many concurrent containers, same way a class spawns many instances
concept_check.explain: An image is on disk: a tarball of filesystem layers, a config (entrypoint, env, ports), and metadata. A container is a runtime instance: a Linux process running with namespace isolation, started from an image's filesystem. The same image can run as 100 containers concurrently. Forgetting this distinction is the #1 source of confusion for newcomers.

concept_check.q: Why does Docker on macOS / Windows need a Linux VM underneath?
choices: Containers are Linux kernel features (namespaces, cgroups). They cannot run natively on the macOS or Windows kernels. Docker Desktop ships a tiny Linux VM (HyperKit / WSL2) and runs containers inside that
concept_check.explain: Containers aren't a VM technology; they're a Linux kernel feature stack, namespaces (isolation) + cgroups (resource limits) + chroot-like filesystem views. macOS and Windows kernels don't have those primitives. Docker Desktop solves this by running a small Linux VM in the background and forwarding `docker` commands into it. That's why your laptop's `docker run` is technically running on Linux even when you're on macOS.

concept_check.q: Why are Dockerfile layers cached?
choices: Each instruction becomes a layer. If the inputs to a layer haven't changed since last build, Docker reuses the cached output, making rebuilds 10-100x faster. Order instructions so slow-changing things (apt-installs) come BEFORE fast-changing things (your source code)
concept_check.explain: Every Dockerfile instruction produces a content-addressed layer. Docker hashes the layer's inputs (the parent layer + the instruction + the files COPY'd in); if that hash matches a previously-built layer, the cached layer is reused. Edit one line of source code: only the COPY-source-code layer and everything after it rebuilds. Edit the Dockerfile to add a system package: the apt layer and everything after it rebuilds. Ordering matters, put slow, stable stuff (FROM, system deps) FIRST; fast-changing stuff (source code) LAST.

days.title: A container is not a tiny VM
days.summary: Process isolation via Linux kernel features. Watch the canonical 100-second intro.

items.title: The kernel-features mental model
items.body:
## The pitch
A container is one or more Linux processes running with:
- A private view of the filesystem (chroot-like).
- A private view of the process tree (`pid` namespace, `ps aux` inside shows ONLY container processes).
- A private network stack (`net` namespace, own IP, own ports).
- A private hostname (`uts` namespace).
- Resource limits enforced by cgroups (max RAM, max CPU shares).

That's it. No emulated hardware. No second kernel. Just the host kernel exposing isolated views of itself per container.

## Container vs VM
```text
VM Container
──── ─────────
Hypervisor (KVM, ESXi) Container runtime (containerd)
Guest kernel Shared host kernel
Boots in seconds Starts in milliseconds
~GB image ~MB image
Strong isolation Process-level isolation
Heavy, slow Light, fast
```

## What you build this week
By Sunday:
- A multi-stage Dockerfile for a Node.js (or static site) build
- An image tagged + pushed to Docker Hub
- Run it locally with `docker run -p 8080:80 yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0`
- A working README so anyone clones + runs in 30 seconds

## The killer property
"Works on my machine" stops being a sentence anyone can say. The image runs identically on macOS / Windows / Linux / CI / production.

items.title: Install + verify
items.body:
## Install Docker Desktop
- **macOS**: download from docker.com/products/docker-desktop. Drag to Applications. Launch.
- **Windows**: ensure WSL2 enabled, install from same URL.
- **Linux**: native `docker` package or Docker Desktop for Linux (newer).

After install, in a fresh terminal:
```bash
docker --version
# Docker version 27.x ...

docker run hello-world
```
You should see the welcome message. If you do, Docker is working end-to-end (image pulled from Docker Hub, container ran, output captured).

## The five commands you'll use most
```bash
docker pull IMAGE # download an image
docker run -p HOST:CONT IMAGE # run a container, map ports
docker ps # list running containers
docker logs CONTAINER # see its output
docker stop CONTAINER # graceful stop (SIGTERM)
```

## Run a real image, nginx
```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
# -d detached (background)
# --name give it a friendly name
# -p 8080:80 map host port 8080 to container port 80
```

Open http://localhost:8080, you'll see the nginx welcome page. Inside a Docker container. Running. Just like that.

```bash
docker ps # confirms it's running
docker logs web # nginx access logs
docker stop web # graceful stop
docker rm web # remove the container record
```

## Inspect the container's worldview
```bash
# spin one up again, this time exec into it
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
docker exec -it web sh
# inside the container now
ps aux # only the nginx process, pid namespace at work
ls / # alpine root, different from your host
hostname # synthetic name like '7f3a2c...'
exit
```

Different process list. Different filesystem. Different hostname. All on your machine. The namespaces in action.

cards.whenWrong: Yes, `exec -it` is the get-inside command. Useful for debugging.

cards.whenRight: Right, `docker stop` sends SIGTERM (graceful), waits 10s, THEN SIGKILL. `docker kill` is immediate.

items.title: Dockerfile basics
items.body:
## The smallest useful Dockerfile (Node app)
```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine # base image, minimal Linux + Node 20
WORKDIR /app # cd into /app inside the container
COPY package*.json ./ # copy lockfiles ONLY first
RUN npm ci --only=production # install deps from lockfile
COPY . . # copy the rest of the source
EXPOSE 3000 # documentation; doesn't actually publish
CMD ["node", "server.js"] # default command when container starts
```

## Why two COPYs?
Cache discipline. The first `COPY package*.json` + `RUN npm ci` becomes a cached layer keyed on the lockfile. If lockfile didn't change → npm install is skipped on rebuild. Source code changes in the second `COPY . .`, only that layer and downstream layers rebuild. Saves 30+ seconds on every iteration.

## For a static site (Edge Portfolio)
```dockerfile
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
# optional: copy a custom nginx.conf if needed
EXPOSE 80
# CMD inherits nginx's default, runs the daemon
```

That's the WHOLE build. nginx:alpine is ~50MB; this image adds ~1KB. Done.

## Build it
```bash
# from your repo root
docker build -t edge-portfolio:0.1 .
# tag image as edge-portfolio:0.1
# trailing . = build context (current directory)
```

Docker uploads the context to the daemon, runs each instruction, produces a layered image. Watch the output, each line shows a layer cache hit or rebuild.

## Run it
```bash
docker run -d --name portfolio -p 8080:80 edge-portfolio:0.1
# Open http://localhost:8080, your portfolio served by nginx in a container
```

## The .dockerignore, non-optional
Create `.dockerignore` in repo root:
```
node_modules
.git
.github
*.md
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
```
Without this, `COPY . .` copies your `.git` directory, your local `node_modules`, everything. Image bloats 10x. ALWAYS .dockerignore.

cards.prompt: `COPY package*.json ./` before `COPY . .` is a layer-cache optimisation, not a syntax requirement.
cards.whenRight: Right, semantically equivalent to one COPY, but enables npm install to be cached when lockfile didn't change.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, cache discipline. Slow stable stuff first; fast-changing last. Iteration time drops dramatically.

cards.prompt: A missing `.dockerignore` can balloon image size 10x.
cards.whenRight: Right, `.git` alone is often hundreds of MB. node_modules too. Always .dockerignore.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, set it once, save GB. Single highest-leverage file in any Docker repo.

cards.prompt: `EXPOSE 80` in a Dockerfile actually publishes port 80 to your host.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. `EXPOSE` is documentation. `-p` on `docker run` is what publishes.
cards.whenWrong: EXPOSE = documentation. `-p 8080:80` on `docker run` is what actually maps the port.

days.title: Multi-stage builds
days.summary: Build with heavy tools; ship only the runtime.

items.title: Why multi-stage
items.body:
## The problem
For a TypeScript or webpack-built app, you need a node + npm + dev-deps environment to BUILD the bundle. But the runtime only needs the bundle + maybe a tiny static server.

Single-stage: image ships 800MB of devDependencies and a node toolchain it never uses.

Multi-stage: separate the build environment from the runtime image; only the bundle ships.

## The pattern
```dockerfile
# ───── Stage 1: build ─────
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci # devDeps included for the build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build # output e.g. /app/dist

# ───── Stage 2: runtime ─────
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
```

Two `FROM`s = two stages. Final image is based on the LAST stage only; intermediate stage gets discarded.

## What you ship
```text
Single-stage with node:20: ~1 GB
Multi-stage with nginx:alpine: ~50 MB (nginx base) + your bundle
```

20x smaller image. Faster pulls. Smaller attack surface (no node + npm in prod).

## For a Node API (runtime that DOES need node)
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --production

FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./package.json
USER node # non-root
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

Two stages, final image has only production deps + the compiled output. ~150MB instead of ~1.2GB.

## Build + verify
```bash
docker build -t edge-portfolio:0.2 .
docker image ls edge-portfolio # check the SIZE column
```

Compare before/after sizes. Real numbers; visible win.

cards.prompt: Multi-stage builds discard intermediate stages from the final image.
cards.whenRight: Right, only the LAST stage ships. Intermediate stages exist during build only.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, last stage = the shipped image. Earlier stages are scratchpads, discarded.

cards.prompt: A 20x size reduction is realistic when moving from single-stage to multi-stage.
cards.whenRight: Right, typical for TypeScript/webpack projects. Dev tools alone are GB.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, 10-50x reduction is common. The build toolchain is heavy; the runtime usually isn't.

cards.prompt: Smaller images are only a cost optimisation; security doesn't matter.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Fewer packages = smaller attack surface = fewer CVEs to patch. Real security gain.
cards.whenWrong: Both cost AND security. Every package in the image is a potential CVE. Minimise.

days.title: Persistence + multi-container basics
days.summary: Volumes for data; preview compose without diving deep.

items.title: Volumes, when state matters
items.body:
## Why containers + state is tricky
Containers are EPHEMERAL by design. Kill the container, you lose its filesystem.

Most app data shouldn't live in the container, it should live in a Docker VOLUME or be mounted from the host.

## Three storage flavours
```text
1. Container layer (default)
 Writable layer attached to the container.
 Vanishes on docker rm.
 Use only for temp / cache data you don't care about.

2. Bind mount
 Mount a HOST directory into the container.
 docker run -v /host/path:/container/path ...
 Best for dev: edit on host, container sees changes immediately.

3. Named volume
 Docker-managed storage with a name.
 docker volume create mydata
 docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/data ...
 Best for prod data (Postgres, etc), survives container removal,
 no host filesystem layout coupling.
```

## See it in action, Postgres with a named volume
```bash
docker volume create pg-data

docker run -d --name pg \
 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
 -v pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
 -p 5432:5432 \
 postgres:16-alpine

# create a row
docker exec -it pg psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE t (x int); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);"

# nuke the container
docker stop pg && docker rm pg

# start a NEW container with the same volume
docker run -d --name pg \
 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
 -v pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
 -p 5432:5432 \
 postgres:16-alpine

# data is still there
docker exec -it pg psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM t;"
# x 
# ---
# 1
```

The container died; the volume persisted. That's how stateful services work in Docker.

## What about multi-container apps?
A real app = api + db + cache, all running together. Doing this with raw `docker run` is painful (network setup, dependency ordering). That's what Docker Compose solves, entire topic next week (W6).

cards.prompt: Data written to a container's filesystem (no volume) survives `docker rm`.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Container layer vanishes with the container. Use volumes for anything you want to keep.
cards.whenWrong: Lost. Container layer is ephemeral. Volumes / bind mounts / external storage for anything persistent.

cards.prompt: Bind mounts are best for dev; named volumes are best for production state.
cards.whenRight: Right, bind = host-coupled; great for live-reload. Named = managed by Docker; portable across hosts.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, bind for dev iteration, named for prod data. Different tools for different jobs.

cards.prompt: Running Postgres in a container with a named volume is reasonable for development.
cards.whenRight: Right, entirely. Pin a version, mount the volume, get the same DB everywhere. Standard pattern.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, totally reasonable for dev. Production is a separate decision (managed RDS often beats self-hosted).

days.title: Registries, push to Docker Hub
days.summary: Public image that anyone can pull.

items.title: Tag + push
items.body:
## The flow
```text
local image ──[tag with registry prefix]──> registry-qualified name ──[push]──> Docker Hub
```

## Step 1, Docker Hub account
Sign up at hub.docker.com (free). Note your username; e.g. `yourname`.

## Step 2, login
```bash
docker login
# enter username + password
# (or use a Personal Access Token from Account Settings → Security)
```

## Step 3, tag your image
```bash
# the image you built locally
docker image ls edge-portfolio

# add a registry-qualified tag
docker tag edge-portfolio:0.2 yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
docker tag edge-portfolio:0.2 yourname/edge-portfolio:latest # convention
```

## Step 4, push
```bash
docker push yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
docker push yourname/edge-portfolio:latest
```

Each layer uploads to Hub. Existing layers (nginx:alpine base) are deduplicated, only YOUR layers actually upload.

## Verify
Visit https://hub.docker.com/r/yourname/edge-portfolio, your image page appears with the tags.

## Anyone can now pull and run
```bash
docker pull yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
docker run -d -p 8080:80 yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
```

That's distribution. From your laptop to anyone's machine in a single command.

## Tagging conventions
```text
yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0 # specific version
yourname/edge-portfolio:1 # major-version pin
yourname/edge-portfolio:latest # 'most recent' floating
yourname/edge-portfolio:sha-abc123 # git-sha pin for reproducibility
```

For production: pin to a specific tag (not `latest`). `latest` is a moving target; pinning is reproducibility.

cards.prompt: `latest` is a safe tag for production deployments.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. `latest` is a moving target. Pin to a specific version or git-sha for reproducible deploys.
cards.whenWrong: Pin specifically. `latest` changes under you and breaks deploys.

cards.prompt: Pushing to Docker Hub uploads layers that the registry already has.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Layers are content-addressed; existing ones are deduplicated; only new layers actually upload.
cards.whenWrong: Dedup. Public base layers (nginx:alpine) are already on Hub; you only upload YOUR layers.

cards.prompt: Once an image is on Docker Hub, anyone can `docker pull` it.
cards.whenRight: Right, if it's public. Private repos require auth.
cards.whenWrong: Public images: anyone, no auth. Private: requires login. Default for free tier = public.

- Multi-stage build: build with node:20-alpine, ship only the static dist
- Final size: ~52 MB (visible in `docker image ls`)

## Registry
hub.docker.com/r/yourname/edge-portfolio
Tags: 1.0, 1, latest

## Quickstart

## Honest limitations
- nginx serves on port 80 as root inside the container, for a static site
 this is fine but generally we'd run as non-root user (W7 will harden this).
- No image-signing yet (W7).
- No vulnerability scan in CI yet (W7).
```

## Tag and ship
```bash
git add Dockerfile .dockerignore DOCKER.md README.md
git commit -m 'docs: containerisation writeup'
git tag v1.0
git push && git push --tags
```

## What you can now claim
- Public site at yourdomain.com (v0.2).
- Automated CI/CD on every push (v0.3).
- Real monitoring with alarms (v0.4).
- Containerised + on Docker Hub (v1.0).

That's a full ops loop on one project. From here W6-W7 deepen the container story (Compose for multi-service; hardening for security).

weeks.title: Docker Compose, Local Dev, and the Inner Loop
weeks.context:
Docker Compose is the tool for running multi-container applications locally. Your production application is rarely just one process, it is a web server, a database, a cache, maybe a background worker. Docker Compose lets you define all of these as services in a single YAML file and start them all with docker compose up. Each service runs in its own container; they communicate over a shared Docker network.

The inner loop in software development is the cycle of: edit code, see the change, iterate. The inner loop speed determines how fast you can develop. With Docker Compose and volume mounts, you can have the best of both worlds: a consistent, containerised environment (no "works on my machine") and fast iteration (changes to source code are reflected immediately without rebuilding the image, because the source code directory is mounted from the host into the container).

docker-compose.yml structure: services (each service is a container), networks (custom networks for container communication), volumes (persistent storage). Key service options: image or build (pre-built image or build from Dockerfile), ports (host:container port mapping), environment (environment variables), depends_on (service startup order), volumes (volume mounts).

Health checks in Docker Compose: the depends_on option only waits for the container to start, not for the application inside to be ready. Your Node app starting before PostgreSQL is ready causes connection errors. Add a healthcheck to the postgres service (pg_isready -U postgres) and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy.

The production question: Docker Compose is for local development and single-server deployments. For production with multiple servers, you use Kubernetes (W9). But for a small application on a single server, Docker Compose in production is completely valid, many successful startups run on Docker Compose for years.

concept_check.q: Why does Compose make multi-container apps easier than raw `docker run`?
choices: One YAML file declares every service + network + volume. `docker compose up` creates them all with one command, in the right order, on a shared network. `docker run` requires manual networking + dependency management for every container
concept_check.explain: Raw `docker run`: create a network, run postgres with -v + -p + --network, wait for it to be ready, run redis with --network, wait, run api with --network --link or env vars pointing at postgres + redis... five terminal commands per restart. Compose makes that one YAML + one command. Plus services on the same Compose network can address each other by name (`postgres`, `redis`) instead of IP. Same primitives; sane orchestration.

concept_check.q: Why use a bind mount on source code for dev but bake source INTO the image for production?
choices: Bind mount = live reload on host file changes (fast inner loop). Image-baked = immutable, reproducible, no host coupling (deployable artifact). Different optimisations for different phases of the workflow
concept_check.explain: Dev needs fast iteration: edit, see change. Bind mount mounts your local source into the container so file changes propagate without rebuilding. Production needs reproducibility + portability: the image must contain everything it needs, identical on every host. Different stages, different storage strategies, both right for their context.

concept_check.q: Why does `depends_on: { condition: service_healthy }` matter beyond just `depends_on`?
choices: `depends_on` only waits for the dependent CONTAINER to START, not for the application inside to be READY. `service_healthy` waits until the healthcheck passes, which actually means 'ready to accept connections'
concept_check.explain: Container started ≠ Postgres accepting connections. A typical bug: api container starts immediately after postgres container starts, tries to connect, gets refused, crashes. `service_healthy` gates on the healthcheck (e.g. `pg_isready -U postgres`); only when that passes does the api container start. Eliminates the race.

items.title: Compose in one breath
items.body:
## The problem
Your local dev needs: web app + Postgres + Redis + maybe MailHog for email testing. With raw Docker, that's:
```bash
docker network create app-net
docker volume create pg-data
docker run -d --name pg --network app-net -v pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16
docker run -d --name redis --network app-net redis:7-alpine
docker run -d --name mail --network app-net -p 8025:8025 mailhog/mailhog
docker run -d --name api --network app-net -p 3000:3000 -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:secret@pg:5432/postgres -e REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379 myapp:dev
```
Five commands. Half a dozen flags each. Memorise the connection URLs. Re-type after every reboot.

## The Compose version
```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
 pg:
 image: postgres:16
 environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret }
 volumes: [pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
 redis:
 image: redis:7-alpine
 mail:
 image: mailhog/mailhog
 ports: ['8025:8025']
 api:
 build: .
 ports: ['3000:3000']
 environment:
 DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@pg:5432/postgres
 REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
 depends_on: [pg, redis]

volumes:
 pg-data:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d # everything, one command
docker compose logs -f api # follow the api logs
docker compose down # stop + remove everything
```

That's it. The YAML is the source of truth for what your dev environment IS.

## What you ship this week
`docker-compose.yml` for a real two-service setup (Node API + Postgres):
- API live-reloads on source change (bind mount).
- Postgres persists data via named volume.
- Healthcheck on Postgres; API waits for it.
- Env vars in a `.env` file (NOT committed).
- `docker compose up` brings the whole world up in <10 seconds.

cards.prompt: Services in the same Compose file can address each other by service name (e.g. `pg:5432`).
cards.whenRight: Right, Compose creates a default network; service names become DNS names on it.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, service name = DNS name on the Compose network. Don't hardcode IPs.

cards.prompt: `docker compose down` deletes named volumes by default.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Volumes survive. Use `down -v` if you really want to nuke them.
cards.whenWrong: Survives. `down` removes containers + network; volumes persist unless you pass `-v`.

cards.prompt: Compose is suitable for small production deploys on a single VM.
cards.whenRight: Right, many companies run Compose in prod on a single VM for years. K8s only matters at scale.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, totally valid prod stack at small scale. K8s only when you outgrow it.

days.title: Write your first compose.yml
days.summary: Two services: a small Node API + Postgres.

items.title: docker-compose.yml, minimal real version
items.body:
## File
```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
 pg:
 image: postgres:16-alpine
 restart: unless-stopped
 environment:
 POSTGRES_USER: app
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
 POSTGRES_DB: app
 volumes:
 - pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
 ports:
 - '5432:5432'
 healthcheck:
 test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U app -d app']
 interval: 5s
 timeout: 3s
 retries: 5

 api:
 build:
 context: .
 dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev # see day 3 for this file
 restart: unless-stopped
 environment:
 DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@pg:5432/app
 NODE_ENV: development
 ports:
 - '3000:3000'
 depends_on:
 pg:
 condition: service_healthy

volumes:
 pg-data:
```

## Bring it up
```bash
docker compose up -d # detached
docker compose ps # what's running
docker compose logs -f api # follow api logs
docker compose down # stop + remove containers (volume survives)
```

## Test connectivity
```bash
# from your host
psql postgres://app:app@localhost:5432/app -c 'SELECT 1;'

# OR from inside the api container
docker compose exec api sh
# inside container
node -e "const {Client}=require('pg'); const c=new Client({connectionString:process.env.DATABASE_URL}); c.connect().then(()=>c.query('SELECT 1')).then(r=>{console.log(r.rows); process.exit();})"
```

## Why the healthcheck matters here
Without `depends_on: { condition: service_healthy }`, the api starts the moment the pg CONTAINER is up, typically before pg is actually accepting connections. The api crashes on first DB query. The healthcheck eliminates this race.

cards.prompt: `restart: unless-stopped` makes the container come back up after `docker compose down`.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. `unless-stopped` covers crashes + host reboots, but `compose down` is an explicit stop.
cards.whenWrong: Explicit stops are respected. `restart` covers crashes + boots, not deliberate stops.

cards.prompt: Compose creates a default network for services in the file; they reach each other by service name.
cards.whenRight: Right, the api can connect to `pg:5432`, not an IP. Compose-managed DNS.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, service-name DNS. Don't hardcode IPs; reach by name.

cards.prompt: The healthcheck on Postgres is paranoid, `depends_on` alone is enough.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. `depends_on` only waits for container START, not for readiness. Healthcheck makes 'ready' real.
cards.whenWrong: depends_on = container started, NOT app ready. Healthcheck is what gates on actual readiness.

days.title: Bind-mount source for live reload
days.summary: Dev Dockerfile + volume mount = hot reload without rebuild.

items.title: Dockerfile.dev + bind mount
items.body:
## The dev Dockerfile
```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.dev
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci # install ALL deps including dev
# DO NOT COPY source code here, it comes via bind mount
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev"] # e.g. nodemon
```

`npm run dev` should run something like nodemon that watches the filesystem and restarts the process on file change.

## docker-compose.yml, add the bind mount
Update the `api` service:
```yaml
 api:
 build:
 context: .
 dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev
 environment:
 DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@pg:5432/app
 NODE_ENV: development
 ports:
 - '3000:3000'
 volumes:
 - .:/app # bind mount source ← THIS
 - /app/node_modules # anonymous volume preserves container's node_modules
 depends_on:
 pg:
 condition: service_healthy
```

## Why two volume lines
- `.:/app`, your local repo mounted at /app in the container. Edit on host → container sees instantly.
- `/app/node_modules`, anonymous volume that 'masks' the host's node_modules. Without it, the host's (possibly empty or wrong-arch) node_modules would shadow the container's.

This is the magic pattern for Node + Docker.

## Try it
```bash
docker compose up -d --build # --build rebuilds the image after Dockerfile.dev change
docker compose logs -f api # nodemon waiting for changes

# In another terminal, edit a file in your repo
# Save
# Watch nodemon restart in the logs window, INSIDE the container
```

Fast inner loop, identical environment, no host node version pain.

cards.prompt: Bind-mounting source code is fine for production deploys.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Prod images bake the code in for immutability + reproducibility. Bind mounts are dev-only.
cards.whenWrong: Dev only. Prod = baked-in, immutable, reproducible. Different optimisation; different storage strategy.

cards.prompt: The anonymous `/app/node_modules` volume prevents your host's node_modules from masking the container's.
cards.whenRight: Right, classic gotcha. Without it, the container's node_modules disappears under the host bind mount.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, anonymous volume preserves the container's node_modules. Without it, fresh-install agony.

cards.prompt: After editing source, you must `docker compose restart api` for the change to apply.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. If you've configured nodemon or similar, the file change is detected automatically.
cards.whenWrong: Nodemon (or equivalent) auto-restarts. The whole point of the bind mount.

items.title: .env discipline in Compose
items.body:
## The pattern
Compose auto-reads a file called `.env` in the project root. Variables there can be referenced in `docker-compose.yml` with `${VAR}` syntax.

## .env (NEVER COMMIT)
```
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=this-is-only-for-dev
POSTGRES_DB=app
JWT_SECRET=dev-only-secret-rotate-for-prod
```

## .env.example (COMMIT)
```
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me
POSTGRES_DB=app
JWT_SECRET=change-me
```

## .gitignore, add `.env`
```
.env
```

## docker-compose.yml, reference vars
```yaml
services:
 pg:
 image: postgres:16-alpine
 environment:
 POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER}
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
 POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB}
 # ... rest unchanged
 api:
 environment:
 DATABASE_URL: postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@pg:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}
 JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET}
 NODE_ENV: development
```

## Bring up + verify
```bash
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env with your dev values
docker compose up -d
docker compose config # shows the resolved compose with vars substituted (no secrets in stdout)
```

## Why .env.example
Anyone cloning your repo runs `cp .env.example .env`, edits, and goes. Zero guessing about which env vars are required. Same .env discipline as W1 of AI-eng, applied here for Compose.

cards.prompt: `.env` should be committed so teammates can run the project.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. .env has REAL values (passwords). Commit .env.example (placeholders) instead.
cards.whenWrong: Never. .env is gitignored. .env.example is the contract; teammates copy + edit.

cards.prompt: `docker compose config` prints the YAML with env vars resolved.
cards.whenRight: Right, useful for debugging substitution. Watch for missing values (shows as blank).
cards.whenWrong: Yes, config = resolved view. Great for verifying env vars wired correctly.

cards.prompt: Production should reuse the dev `.env` file.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Prod env vars come from the deploy target's secrets store, never from a dev file.
cards.whenWrong: Different .env per env. Prod values from a secrets manager; dev values from local file.

days.title: Healthchecks for the API too
days.summary: Self-report 'ready' so other services can wait.

items.title: API healthcheck + readiness
items.body:
## Why
A real api dies on bad DB connection during boot, fails to respond, or returns errors. A healthcheck makes the container's readiness MACHINE-CHECKABLE.

## Implement /healthz in your app
```js
// in your api server (Express example)
app.get('/healthz', async (req, res) => {
 try {
 await db.query('SELECT 1'); // confirm DB reachable
 res.status(200).json({ ok: true });
 } catch (e) {
 res.status(503).json({ ok: false, error: e.message });
 }
});
```

`/healthz` returns 200 ONLY when the api is fully operational (can talk to its dependencies). Returns 503 if not.

## Add to docker-compose.yml
```yaml
 api:
 # ... existing ...
 healthcheck:
 test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'wget -q -O /dev/null http://localhost:3000/healthz || exit 1']
 interval: 10s
 timeout: 3s
 retries: 3
 start_period: 15s # grace period for the app to start before failures count
```

`start_period` gives the api 15s to come up cleanly before failing healthchecks count as down, important for slow-starting apps.

## See it in `docker compose ps`
```
NAME STATUS PORTS
api Up 12 seconds (healthy) 0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp
pg Up 12 seconds (healthy) 0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp
```

`(healthy)` next to status. If your reverse proxy or load balancer reads Docker health state, it can route around unhealthy backends automatically.

## Why this matters for prod
Kubernetes uses the same concept (`readinessProbe`, `livenessProbe`). Building the healthcheck discipline in Compose now means K8s migration is trivial later.

cards.prompt: /healthz should return 200 OK even if the database connection is broken.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Liveness should be honest. If you can't talk to your DB, you're not healthy.
cards.whenWrong: False positive = traffic routes to a broken instance. /healthz lies = outage.

cards.prompt: `start_period` prevents healthcheck failures from counting against the container during initial boot.
cards.whenRight: Right, graceful boot window. Without it, slow-starting apps die before they're ready.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, boot grace. Essential for any app whose startup takes more than a few seconds.

cards.prompt: Compose healthchecks translate directly to Kubernetes readiness/liveness probes.
cards.whenRight: Right, same concept, same intent. K8s probes are richer, but if you've practiced in Compose, K8s is a small jump.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, Compose's healthcheck is the conceptual seed of K8s probes. Practice here transfers.

6. Restart pg; api returns to healthy.

days.title: Compose vs prod orchestrators, when to graduate
days.summary: Compose stays good until it doesn't.

items.title: When Compose stops being right
items.body:
## Compose is excellent for
- Local dev for any team size
- CI integration tests (`docker compose up -d`, run tests, `down`)
- Single-server production for small apps (yes really, many startups run Compose in prod for years)

## Compose becomes the wrong tool when
```text
- You need to deploy to MULTIPLE servers (Compose runs on one host).
- You need auto-scaling based on load.
- You need rolling deploys with zero downtime.
- You need a control plane (declarative desired state with self-healing).
```

At THAT scale, you move to Kubernetes (or AWS ECS / Fargate / Nomad / etc.).

## The migration story
Compose → Kubernetes manifests is mostly mechanical:
```text
Compose service K8s primitive
──────────────── ─────────────
service Deployment + Service
image containers.image
environment env / envFrom
ports containerPort + Service.port
volumes (named) PersistentVolumeClaim + volumeMount
volumes (bind) emptyDir or ConfigMap (no host coupling)
healthcheck readinessProbe + livenessProbe
depends_on (healthy) initContainers or readiness gating
```

Each Compose service maps to roughly 2-3 K8s manifests. Tools like `kompose` automate the bulk of the conversion.

## The wrong reason to graduate
"Resume" or "because everyone uses K8s". K8s is heavy. If you don't NEED its scale features, you're paying its complexity for nothing. Compose-on-one-VM with a healthcheck-gated reverse proxy serves real traffic at small scale.

## Stay calm
Most ML / data / web teams reach $10M ARR on Compose or simple ECS/Fargate. K8s is the migration FROM that, not the destination from day one.

items.title: kompose, Compose to Kubernetes converter

cards.whenWrong: Start simple. K8s pre-scale = paying complexity for no value. Migrate when forced.

items.title: COMPOSE.md + tag
items.body:
## COMPOSE.md
```markdown
# Local dev stack, Docker Compose

## Services
- **pg** (postgres:16-alpine), main database, named volume `pg-data`
- **api** (built from `Dockerfile.dev`), Node.js api with bind-mounted source for hot reload

## Bring up
```bash
cp .env.example .env # edit values
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api # follow logs
```

API: http://localhost:3000
Postgres: localhost:5432 (user: app / pass: from .env)

## Hot reload
Source is bind-mounted into the api container. Save a `.ts` / `.js` file in the repo, nodemon detects + restarts INSIDE the container.

## Healthchecks
- pg: `pg_isready` every 5s
- api: GET `/healthz` every 10s (start_period 15s)
- `docker compose ps` shows `(healthy)` next to status when both are operational

## Reset DB
```bash
docker compose down -v # wipes the pg-data volume
docker compose up -d
```

## When to migrate off Compose
See [MIGRATION.md](MIGRATION.md). Short version: when you need multi-host or auto-scaling, move to K8s.
```

## Tag
```bash
git add docker-compose.yml Dockerfile.dev .env.example .gitignore COMPOSE.md MIGRATION.md
git commit -m 'docker: dev stack via Compose + healthchecks + hot reload'
git tag compose-v1
git push && git push --tags
```

## What you've built this week
- One-command up of a real multi-service dev environment
- Live source reload, fast inner loop
- Real healthchecks + readiness gating between services
- .env discipline that translates to every deploy target
- Honest writeup of when to graduate to K8s

That's a real-team dev experience, reproducible across machines.

cards.whenWrong: Worth it. Future-you thanks you; recruiters notice operational thinking.

cards.prompt: Documenting WHEN to migrate to K8s is a senior-DevOps signal.
cards.whenRight: Right, naming the migration trigger means you understand the tradeoffs.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, engineers who name the trigger are engineers who picked the right tool now.

cards.prompt: Once Compose is in place, you never need Dockerfile.dev, the api runs from source.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Dockerfile.dev defines the BASE (node version, npm install) that the bind mount layers on.
cards.whenWrong: Dockerfile.dev = base layer. Bind mount = code overlay. Both required.

weeks.title: Image Hardening, Security Scanning, and Supply Chain
weeks.context:
Every container image you run in production is a potential security vulnerability. The base image (node:20-alpine) contains the entire Alpine Linux operating system plus Node.js, hundreds of packages, any of which might have a known CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). Your application code adds more dependencies. Image hardening and security scanning are the practices that reduce this attack surface.

Image hardening: making the image as small and secure as possible. Use minimal base images (Alpine or Distroless). Remove build tools from the final image (multi-stage builds). Do not install packages you do not use. Run as a non-root user. Do not include secrets in the image (they end up in docker history and any image layer inspector). Read-only filesystem (--read-only flag at runtime) prevents attackers from modifying files inside a running container.

Distroless images: built by Google. They contain only the application runtime (Node.js) and its dependencies, no shell, no package manager, no system utilities. This is the most secure image type. The tradeoff: debugging is harder (no shell to exec into). Use Distroless in production; use a regular Alpine image in development.

Software supply chain security is the practice of ensuring the code and dependencies you are running are what you think they are. npm packages can be compromised (malicious code added to a legitimate package, the left-pad incident, the event-stream incident). Docker images from Docker Hub may be modified. Practices: pin image versions exactly (sha256 digest, not just a tag), use npm ci (installs exactly what is in package-lock.json), audit dependencies regularly (npm audit), and use a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to track what is in your image.

Trivy is a free, comprehensive vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems, and Kubernetes. Run trivy image myapp:1.0.0 to scan for CVEs in the image. Trivy checks the base image, installed packages, and language-specific dependencies (npm, pip, Gemfile). It categorises findings by severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, UNKNOWN. Fix CRITICAL and HIGH; evaluate MEDIUM; document why you accepted LOW.

concept_check.q: Why is running as non-root inside a container important even though the container is isolated?
choices: If an attacker exploits your app, they inherit the in-container user's privileges. Root-in-container + a kernel CVE = root-on-host. Non-root limits the blast radius even when containment fails
concept_check.explain: Container isolation isn't perfect. Multiple historical CVEs (CVE-2019-5736, CVE-2022-0492, container escape via runc) let root-in-container break out to root-on-host. Running as non-root means: even if your app is exploited AND there's a container-escape CVE, the attacker only gets non-root on the host, still very bad, but a hard upgrade for them. Defence in depth.

concept_check.q: Why pin Docker image tags to a digest (`sha256:...`) instead of a version tag?
choices: Tags are MUTABLE, `nginx:1.25` can be re-tagged at the registry to point at a different image any day. A digest is content-addressed: the bytes don't change. Pinning to digest = truly reproducible builds + cryptographic guarantee of what you're running
concept_check.explain: A tag is a pointer maintained by whoever publishes the image. `nginx:1.25` today might be `sha256:abc...`; tomorrow the publisher updates it to `sha256:def...` with a security patch. Sometimes great; sometimes you're now running unverified code. A digest pin (`nginx:1.25@sha256:abc...`) anchors to the exact bytes you've audited. Production images SHOULD use digest pins; humans use tags for ergonomics.

concept_check.q: What does `trivy image` actually scan for?
choices: Three categories: (1) OS packages with known CVEs (Alpine/Debian/RHEL package versions vs CVE DB), (2) language package vulnerabilities (npm / pip / maven dependencies), (3) misconfigurations (running as root, sensitive files, secrets baked in)
concept_check.explain: Trivy reads the image's layers and pulls out: installed OS packages (cross-referenced with NVD / Alpine secdb / Debian DSA), language-specific lockfiles inside (npm + pip + go.sum), Dockerfile patterns (running as root, ADD with remote URLs), and even secrets that got baked in via misclicked .dockerignore. One scan, multiple risk classes. Run it in CI before pushing.

days.title: Orient, threat model
days.summary: What you're actually defending against.

items.title: The container threat model
items.body:
## What containers DON'T protect you from
```text
- A vulnerability in YOUR application code (SQL injection, RCE, etc.)
- A vulnerability in your dependencies (npm package compromise, etc.)
- A vulnerability in the base image's OS packages
- A container ESCAPE CVE in the runtime (runc, containerd, kernel)
- Compromised image at the registry (someone re-pushes nginx:1.25)
```

## What you'll add this week
```text
L1, Minimal base image (Distroless / Alpine) → smaller CVE surface
L2, Run as non-root user → blast radius reduction
L3, Pin image tags by digest → reproducibility + supply-chain integrity
L4, Trivy CVE scan in CI → catch known vulnerabilities pre-deploy
L5, Image signing (cosign) → cryptographic provenance
L6, SBOM generation → know what's actually in the image
```

## What you ship by Sunday
- A hardened Dockerfile (Distroless OR minimal Alpine, non-root user, digest-pinned base)
- Trivy scan in CI: blocks build if CRITICAL CVEs found
- An SBOM (`syft` output) committed for visibility
- (Optional) cosign-signed image pushed to Docker Hub
- A HARDENING.md document explaining choices + tradeoffs

## Why this matters past resume
Most production breaches that get attributed to 'containers' come from this list, not from Docker itself, but from the layers above. Patching at this layer is most teams' biggest defensive wins.

cards.prompt: A container image with no CVEs at build time stays safe forever.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. New CVEs are disclosed daily. Re-scan and rebuild regularly.
cards.whenWrong: Continuous concern. CVE DB updates daily; rebuild + rescan as part of CI cadence.

cards.prompt: Running as root inside a container is fine because containers are isolated.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Container escapes happen. Non-root is the cheap, foundational hardening.
cards.whenWrong: Isolation isn't perfect. Non-root costs ~zero, gains defence-in-depth.

cards.prompt: Image hardening's main value is preventing CVE scanners from flagging your image.
cards.whenRight: Right, opposite. The CVEs are real risks; passing the scanner is just measurement. The reduction IS the value.
cards.whenWrong: Scanner-pass is the symptom; risk reduction is the goal. Don't game the scanner; reduce real risk.

items.body:

1. List the 5 'what containers DON'T protect you from' items in your own words.
2. For each, name ONE concrete control from this week's plan that addresses it.
3. State the week's goal: my Dockerfile is non-root + digest-pinned, my CI fails on CRITICAL CVEs, and an SBOM lives next to the code.

days.title: Distroless or minimal Alpine
days.summary: Less in the image = less attack surface.

items.title: Distroless vs Alpine
items.body:
## Two minimalism schools

### Alpine
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
# ~50 MB. Has busybox shell + apk package manager.
# Debug-friendly: `docker exec -it container sh` works.
```
Trade: still has a shell + package manager → larger CVE surface than distroless.

### Distroless (Google)
```dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
# ~80 MB. NO shell. NO package manager. NO ssh.
# Only the language runtime + your app.
```
Trade: can't `exec sh` for debugging in prod. Use `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12:debug` (has busybox) for troubleshooting only.

## The multi-stage build with distroless
```dockerfile
# Stage 1: build with full toolchain
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --production

# Stage 2: distroless runtime
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./package.json
USER nonroot # distroless provides this user out-of-the-box
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["dist/server.js"] # entrypoint is /usr/bin/node
```

## What you can no longer do (correctly)
```bash
docker exec -it container sh # fails, no shell in distroless
docker exec -it container ls / # fails, no ls
```

Use the `:debug` variant for local debugging; the non-debug variant for prod.

## For a static site (Edge Portfolio)
Distroless equivalent: `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` (~2 MB!). Or you can run nginx as non-root in a small Alpine.

## Build + size compare
```bash
docker build -t myapp:alpine -f Dockerfile.alpine .
docker build -t myapp:distroless -f Dockerfile.distroless .
docker image ls myapp
# REPOSITORY TAG SIZE
# myapp alpine 120 MB
# myapp distroless 95 MB
```

Real numbers; real differences.

items.title: Distroless on GitHub
items.why: Bookmark. Read the README for available variants per language.

cards.prompt: Distroless images include a shell for easy debugging.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. The whole point. Use the `:debug` variant for local troubleshooting.
cards.whenWrong: No shell. Lower attack surface; needs different debug workflow.

cards.prompt: Smaller image = strictly less attack surface.
cards.whenRight: Right, fewer installed packages = fewer CVEs = less to defend.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, every package is a potential CVE. Removing what you don't use is free defence.

cards.prompt: Distroless `:debug` variants should be used in production for emergency access.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Prod runs the slim variant. Debug variant is for staging / dev only.
cards.whenWrong: Debug variant defeats the purpose in prod. Use it for staging or local; prod gets the slim image.

days.title: Non-root user
days.summary: Even if a CVE escapes the container, the attacker doesn't get root on the host.

items.title: Non-root in Dockerfile
items.body:
## Manually create a user (Alpine)
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine

# Create a user and group with predictable UID/GID
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S app && adduser -u 1001 -S app -G app

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --chown=app:app . .

USER app # switch to non-root
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## Why the explicit UID/GID
If you mount a host volume into the container, file ownership uses NUMERIC IDs. Predictable UID/GID lets you align host + container ownership cleanly.

## In distroless (easier)
Distroless images provide a `nonroot` user out of the box:
```dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
USER nonroot # just use it
```

## Common failures and how to fix
```text
 ❌ EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/.cache'
 → your app tries to write somewhere it doesn't own.
 Fix: COPY --chown=app:app on the relevant dir, or pre-mkdir as root.

 ❌ Bind to port 80 fails (only root can bind to <1024)
 → run on a high port (3000+) inside the container.
 Map -p 80:3000 at the host.

 ❌ apt / apk fails during build with non-root user
 → switch back to root for installs:
 USER root
 RUN apk add --no-cache curl
 USER app
```

## Verify
```bash
docker run --rm myapp id
# uid=1001(app) gid=1001(app) groups=1001(app)
```

Not 0. That's the win.

cards.prompt: A container running as root inside is automatically root on the host.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Container namespaces isolate UIDs. Container's root != host's root EXCEPT during a container escape, which is exactly what we're defending against.
cards.whenWrong: Not automatically, but a container-escape CVE turns container-root into host-root in seconds. Non-root closes that gap.

cards.prompt: Non-root containers can listen on port 80 directly.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. <1024 is privileged. Listen on a high port inside; map ports outside.
cards.whenWrong: Map ports. Listen on 3000+ inside the container; `-p 80:3000` at run time.

cards.prompt: Distroless makes non-root easier because it provides a `nonroot` user.
cards.whenRight: Right, `USER nonroot` and you're done. One less line of Dockerfile.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, built-in. One reason distroless is the easier hardening path.

items.title: Your turn, non-root
items.body:
[CODE]
1. Update your Dockerfile to add a user + USER directive (or use distroless's `nonroot`).
2. Build + run; verify `docker exec ... id` shows non-root.
3. Fix any EACCES errors that surface.
4. Confirm the app still works end-to-end.
5. Commit.

days.title: Pin tags by digest
days.summary: Reproducible + supply-chain safe.

items.title: Digest pins
items.body:
## Tags are mutable
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
```
That `20-alpine` tag points at SOME image today. The maintainer can re-tag it tomorrow to point at a different image (typically a security patch, fine). But in principle, anyone who controls the tag can re-target it.

## Digest pins are immutable
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:5a3b9d4f6b8c2d1e9a3f7b2c4d6e8a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f
```
That digest is content-addressed. The bytes ARE that hash. Cannot be re-pointed.

## How to find the current digest
```bash
docker pull node:20-alpine
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' node:20-alpine
# node@sha256:5a3b9d4f...
```

Or just:
```bash
docker manifest inspect node:20-alpine | grep digest
```

## Pin in the Dockerfile
```dockerfile
# Pinned 2026-06-05. Refresh quarterly or when CVE patch needed.
FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:5a3b9d4f6b8c... AS build
# ...
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12@sha256:7e8f9a0b1c2d... AS runtime
# ...
```

## Refresh discipline
- Quarterly: re-fetch tag → grab new digest → update Dockerfile → rebuild → retest.
- On CVE disclosure: refresh immediately for the affected base.
- Use Dependabot / Renovate to automate digest refresh PRs.

## The supply-chain win
Pinning by digest means: even if Docker Hub gets compromised AND your tag gets pointed at malicious content, your build still pulls the original bytes. Cryptographic anchor.

cards.prompt: `node:20-alpine` and `node:20-alpine@sha256:abc...` will always resolve to the same image.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. The tag is a moving pointer; the digest is the actual bytes. Tag can be re-targeted.
cards.whenWrong: Tag mutable, digest immutable. Pin to digest for true reproducibility.

cards.prompt: Dependabot can automate base-image digest refresh PRs.
cards.whenRight: Right, GitHub-native. Set it up; review the weekly PRs; merge after CI.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, Dependabot watches Dockerfile bases. Weekly PRs to refresh digests; easy review.

cards.prompt: Digest-pinning is excessive for non-production projects.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. The discipline cost is one line of Dockerfile + a quarterly refresh. Trivial price for the safety guarantee.
cards.whenWrong: Cheap to do. Even small projects benefit; the discipline scales naturally to teams of any size.

items.title: Your turn, digest pin
items.body:
[CODE]
1. `docker pull node:20-alpine`; grab the digest via `docker inspect`.
2. Update Dockerfile FROMs to use `@sha256:...`.
3. Build + run; confirm same behaviour.
4. (Optional) Enable Dependabot or Renovate for the repo.
5. Document in HARDENING.md when you last refreshed digests.

days.title: Trivy in CI
days.summary: Block builds with CRITICAL CVEs.

items.title: Trivy, the standard scanner
items.body:
## What Trivy scans
- OS packages (Alpine apk, Debian deb)
- Language packages (npm, pip, maven, go.sum, etc.)
- Dockerfile misconfigurations (running as root, ADD with URLs)
- Hardcoded secrets baked into layers

All from one binary.

## Try it locally
```bash
brew install trivy # mac
# or: docker run aquasec/trivy image YOUR-IMAGE

trivy image edge-portfolio:1.0
```

Output: a table per vuln class. Severities: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, UNKNOWN.

## In CI, make it a gate
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: Image security scan
on:
 push: { branches: [main] }
 pull_request:

jobs:
 trivy:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4

 - name: Build image
 run: docker build -t edge-portfolio:scan .

 - name: Trivy scan, fail on CRITICAL
 uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
 with:
 image-ref: edge-portfolio:scan
 format: table
 severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
 exit-code: '1' # fail build on findings
 ignore-unfixed: true # don't fail on CVEs with no patch yet
```

`ignore-unfixed: true` means: if a CVE has no published fix, log it but don't fail. (You can't fix what doesn't have a patch yet; failing on these is pure noise.)

## The trivyignore file
For accepted risks (CVE applies but you've assessed it as not exploitable for your use):
```
# .trivyignore
CVE-2023-12345 # affects only the SMTP path; we don't send email
```

Add a comment with WHY; future-you will want to know.

## Run the gate
Push a commit. Watch the security workflow run. If clean, green. If CRITICAL, red, deploy blocked. Real gate.

cards.prompt: Trivy scans OS packages, language packages, AND misconfigurations.
cards.whenRight: Right, multi-class scanner. One binary; three categories. Great default.
cards.whenWrong: All three. Plus optional secret-scanning. Run it; rely on it.

cards.prompt: `ignore-unfixed: true` hides real risk.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. It hides CVEs with NO published fix yet, those can't be acted on. Real signal stays.
cards.whenWrong: Hides only unactionable noise. Without it, every CI run drowns in unfixable findings.

cards.prompt: A `.trivyignore` file lets you accept specific CVEs after risk assessment.
cards.whenRight: Right, escape hatch for false-positives or accepted-risk CVEs. Document the WHY.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, case-by-case suppression. Always comment WHY; future-you will want to know.

items.title: Your turn, Trivy gate
items.body:
[CODE]
1. Install trivy locally; scan your image; review findings.
2. Add `.github/workflows/security.yml` from the lesson.
3. Push. Confirm the workflow runs.
4. Address any CRITICAL findings (upgrade base, patch deps).
5. Confirm the gate goes green.

days.title: SBOM + supply chain
days.summary: syft for SBOMs; cosign for signing (optional but rare-skill).

items.title: SBOM with syft, sign with cosign
items.body:
## What is an SBOM
Software Bill of Materials: a machine-readable list of every package + version inside an image. SPDX or CycloneDX format.

## Generate one
```bash
# install syft
brew install syft
# or: docker run anchore/syft:latest IMAGE

syft edge-portfolio:1.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

`sbom.json` lists every npm package, every OS package, with versions. Commit it next to your code. Now the world can see EXACTLY what's in your image without pulling it.

## Why this matters
- CISA + executive orders now require SBOMs for federal software.
- Standard ask in security questionnaires.
- Faster CVE response: when a critical CVE drops, you can `grep` SBOMs to find affected images instantly.

## Cosign, image signing (optional)
`cosign` signs images so consumers can cryptographically verify they came from YOU.

```bash
brew install cosign
cosign generate-key-pair # produces cosign.key (PRIVATE!) and cosign.pub

# sign the image after push
docker push yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
cosign sign --key cosign.key yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0

# verify
cosign verify --key cosign.pub yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0
```

## Keyless signing (newer, easier)
```bash
cosign sign yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0 # uses your OIDC identity (GitHub / Google)
```
No key management; the signature is bound to your identity via Sigstore's transparency log. The modern recommended path.

## Why this is a rare hiring signal
Most candidates have never heard of SBOMs or cosign. Doing it on a personal project = senior-ops signal. Worth the 30 minutes.

items.title: Sigstore, cosign docs
items.why: Bookmark. The auth + verify flows are short; the docs are excellent.

cards.prompt: An SBOM is a machine-readable list of every package + version inside an image.
cards.whenRight: Right, SPDX or CycloneDX format. Useful for CVE response + procurement.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, package manifest in a standard format. Easy CVE matching across your fleet.

cards.prompt: Cosign keyless signing requires you to manage a private key file.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Keyless uses your OIDC identity (GitHub / Google) bound to Sigstore's transparency log. No keys to manage.
cards.whenWrong: Keyless = no key file. OIDC-bound signatures. Modern recommended path.

cards.prompt: Generating an SBOM and committing it to the repo is overkill for a personal project.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Strong portfolio signal; almost no candidates do it. 5 minutes of work.
cards.whenWrong: Differentiating. Rare in entry-level portfolios. Cheap; high signal.

items.title: Your turn, SBOM + (optional) sign
items.body:
[CODE]
1. Install syft. `syft yourname/edge-portfolio:1.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json`.
2. Commit sbom.json.
3. (Optional) Install cosign; sign your pushed image; document the public key.
4. Verify locally: `cosign verify --key cosign.pub ...`.
5. NOTES.md: record what surprised you in the SBOM.

days.title: Ship hardened v2.0
days.summary: HARDENING.md + tag.

items.title: HARDENING.md + tag
items.body:
## HARDENING.md
```markdown
# Image hardening

## Defences in place

### L1, Distroless runtime
Final image based on `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12@sha256:...`.
No shell, no package manager, no ssh. ~80 MB.

### L2, Non-root user
`USER nonroot` in the runtime stage. Verified via `docker run --rm img id`.

### L3, Digest-pinned bases
All FROM lines use `@sha256:...` digest pins. Refresh quarterly or on CVE
disclosure. Last refreshed: YYYY-MM-DD.

### L4, CI vulnerability scan
`.github/workflows/security.yml` runs Trivy on every push + PR.
- Fails build on CRITICAL or HIGH (with `ignore-unfixed`).
- Accepted CVEs documented in `.trivyignore` with rationale.

### L5, SBOM
`sbom.json` (CycloneDX) committed; regenerated on every release.

### L6, (Optional) Image signing
Image signed via `cosign sign` (keyless). Public key/verification command
in README.

## Residual risks
- Application-level vulnerabilities (SQL injection, RCE), orthogonal to
 container hardening; addressed by app-level controls.
- A container-escape CVE in the runtime, non-root limits blast radius
 but doesn't eliminate.
- Supply-chain attack against npm, partial defence via lockfile + audit;
 no full mitigation.

## Refresh cadence
- Digest pins: quarterly + on CVE.
- Trivy scan: every CI run.
- SBOM: every release tag.
- npm audit: weekly via Dependabot.
```

## README update
```markdown
## Security
See [HARDENING.md](HARDENING.md). Distroless runtime, non-root user,
digest-pinned bases, Trivy CI gate, SBOM committed.

## Roadmap
- [x] v0.1, bucket + static site
- [x] v0.2, custom domain + HTTPS
- [x] v0.3, automated CI/CD
- [x] v0.4, monitoring + alarms
- [x] v1.0, containerised + on Docker Hub
- [x] v2.0, hardened image + supply chain (you are here)
```

## Tag
```bash
git add HARDENING.md sbom.json .github/workflows/security.yml .trivyignore README.md Dockerfile
git commit -m 'security: hardened image + Trivy gate + SBOM'
git tag v2.0
git push && git push --tags
```

## What you can claim
- Multi-stage build, distroless runtime, non-root user
- Digest-pinned bases with documented refresh cadence
- Vulnerability gate in CI that blocks builds on CRITICAL
- Public SBOM
- HARDENING.md with named residual risks

This is real-team security thinking on a portfolio project. Rare; differentiating.

cards.prompt: Naming residual risks weakens the HARDENING.md.
cards.whenRight: Right, opposite. Named limits = honest engineering. Hidden ones get found.
cards.whenWrong: Strengthens. Specific residual risks = credibility. Vague absolute claims = naivety.

cards.prompt: A refresh cadence (quarterly digest pin updates) is part of the discipline.
cards.whenRight: Right, without cadence, pinned-and-forgotten becomes stale-and-vulnerable.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, pin + refresh. The cadence is the discipline; pinning without it is theatre.

cards.prompt: Most candidates at this level can show: distroless + non-root + digest pin + Trivy gate + SBOM.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Maybe 5% can. That's why doing it differentiates.
cards.whenWrong: Rare. The 5%-can stat is the opportunity; do it and stand out instantly.

[PRODUCE]
1. Write HARDENING.md from the template.
2. Update README with the Security block + roadmap.
3. Commit + tag v2.0 + push tags.

PASS:

[x] security.yml workflow runs Trivy + blocks on CRITICAL
[x] sbom.json committed

[x] HARDENING.md with residual risks named
[x] v2.0 tag pushed

weeks.title: Container Runtime, Beyond Docker, Towards Production
weeks.context:
Docker is a tool, not a standard. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines the standards: the image format and the runtime specification. Docker implements these standards, but so do alternatives: containerd (the container runtime used by Kubernetes), podman (daemon-less, rootless Docker alternative), and runc (the low-level OCI runtime used by Docker and containerd). Understanding the container runtime landscape matters because in production, you are often not using Docker directly, you are using whatever the Kubernetes cluster uses.

containerd is the industry standard container runtime. Docker uses containerd internally. Kubernetes uses containerd. containerd manages the container lifecycle: pulling images, creating containers, starting and stopping them. The Docker CLI sits on top of containerd and adds features like Docker Compose, multi-platform build, and build caching. When you use Kubernetes, you are interacting with containerd directly (via the kubelet), not Docker.

podman is a Docker-compatible CLI that does not require a daemon. Docker uses a central daemon (dockerd) that runs as root. This daemon is a single point of failure and a security risk (if it is compromised, the attacker has root). podman runs containers as the current user (rootless). The CLI is compatible: you can alias docker=podman and most Docker commands work. In enterprise environments (especially Red Hat/OpenShift), podman is the standard.

OCI image format: Docker images are OCI images. An OCI image is a directory structure: a manifest (list of layers), config (the image configuration: environment, CMD, etc.), and layers (tarballs of filesystem changes). When you push an image to a registry, you push the manifest and layers. When you pull, you download the layers and reassemble the filesystem. This is why you can pull images on any OCI-compatible runtime, the format is standardised.

Container networking deep dive: each container gets a virtual network interface (veth pair). One end is in the container; the other is on the host, connected to a bridge network (docker0 by default). The bridge connects all containers and the host. NAT (Network Address Translation) handles communication between the bridge network and the outside world. User-defined networks add DNS resolution (containers can reach each other by name). Host networking (--network=host) removes the isolation, the container shares the host's network namespace.
