items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between a container runtime, a container engine, and a container orchestrator? Container runtime: the low-level component that creates and runs containers using OS primitives (namespaces, cgroups). Examples: runc, crun. Container engine: higher-level software that manages images, volumes, networks, and uses the runtime. Examples: containerd, docker. Container orchestrator: manages multiple containers across multiple servers, handles scheduling, scaling, service discovery. Examples: Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, Nomad. The relationship: Kubernetes (orchestrator) talks to containerd (engine) which uses runc (runtime) to actually run each container.

mastery_questions: What is the difference between a container runtime, a container engine, and a container orchestrator? Container runtime: the low-level component that creates and runs containers using OS primitives (namespaces, cgroups). Examples: runc, crun. Container engine: higher-level software that manages images, volumes, networks, and uses the runtime. Examples: containerd, docker. Container orchestrator: manages multiple containers across multiple servers, handles scheduling, scaling, service discovery. Examples: Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, Nomad. The relationship: Kubernetes (orchestrator) talks to containerd (engine) which uses runc (runtime) to actually run each container.

You are moving from Docker to containerd in a Kubernetes cluster. A developer reports that docker build commands no longer work on the nodes. What happened and what is the fix? Kubernetes uses containerd as the runtime, not the Docker daemon. Docker CLI commands (docker build, docker ps) talk to the Docker daemon, which is not installed or running on the nodes. Developers should not need to SSH into nodes to build or run containers. Builds happen in CI (GitHub Actions, etc.) using Docker or BuildKit, images are pushed to a registry, and Kubernetes pulls from the registry. If you need to interact with containers on a node, use crictl (the CRI-compatible CLI for containerd and other CRI runtimes).

Explain rootless containers. Why do they exist and what are their tradeoffs? Rootless containers run the container runtime and containers as a non-root user. Docker requires root for the daemon (dockerd), this is a security risk because any container escape could give an attacker host root. Podman and containerd's rootless mode use user namespaces to simulate root inside the container while actually running as a non-root user on the host. Tradeoffs: rootless cannot bind to privileged ports (< 1024) without sysctl adjustments. Network performance may be slightly lower (user-space networking). Some operations that require real root are not possible in rootless mode.

What is a container registry and how does image distribution work? A container registry stores OCI images. Docker Hub is the public default. You push: docker push myrepo/myimage:1.0.0. The Docker CLI pushes the image layers to the registry. You pull: docker pull myrepo/myimage:1.0.0 on another machine, the layers are downloaded and reassembled. Registries support content-addressable storage: layers are stored once and shared across images that use the same layer. Private registries (AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Container Registry) require authentication. The registry URL is the image name prefix: ghcr.io/myuser/myimage is on GitHub's registry.

Install podman: podman.io/getting-started/installation. Try running the same commands with podman that you use with docker. Read the OCI Runtime Specification at opencontainers.org/about/overview.
common_mistakes: Assuming Docker and Kubernetes use the same container runtime. Kubernetes does not use the Docker daemon. It uses the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). containerd and CRI-O are CRI implementations. Docker images work in Kubernetes because they are OCI images, the image format is the same.

Building images on Kubernetes nodes. Nodes should only run containers, not build them. Building images requires more privileges, more resources, and is not the node's job. Build in CI, push to a registry, pull in Kubernetes.

Using Docker Hub as your only registry in production. Docker Hub has rate limits (100 pulls per 6 hours for unauthenticated). In production, your Kubernetes cluster pulling images from Docker Hub can hit these limits and fail to start pods. Use a private registry or mirror Docker Hub behind a pull-through cache.

Not understanding the CRI-O vs containerd choice. If you are using OpenShift, CRI-O is the runtime. If you are using standard Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS, or self-managed), containerd is the default. The Kubernetes API is the same; the underlying runtime differences rarely affect application code.

Ignoring container image garbage collection. Over time, unused images accumulate on nodes (especially after frequent deployments). Configure kubelet garbage collection (or containerd's image cleanup policy) to automatically remove images not used by any running container.
weeks.debug_help: crictl commands fail with "unable to connect to CRI runtime": specify the runtime endpoint: crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock ps. The socket path varies by runtime and distribution. podman rootless cannot bind port 80: ports below 1024 require root (or the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start sysctl). Map to a high port in podman (8080:80) and use a firewall rule or nginx on the host to forward port 80 to 8080. Image pull fails in Kubernetes with "ImagePullBackOff": check the error with kubectl describe pod [pod-name], it shows the specific pull error (authentication failure, rate limit, image not found). For private registries, configure an imagePullSecret on the pod or service account.
stretch: Set up a local container registry with Docker Registry (docker pull registry:2 && docker run -p 5000:5000 registry). Push an image to localhost:5000/myimage:latest. Configure Docker to trust this insecure registry (docker daemon config). This is the foundation of air-gapped container deployments.

Explore BuildKit, the modern Docker build system. Build a multi-platform image (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64) using docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64. Push it to a registry and observe that the same image tag serves both architectures. This is how Docker Hub serves images for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

Learn about container security context. Run a container with --security-opt=no-new-privileges and --cap-drop=ALL. Then add back only the capabilities your application needs (--cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind to low ports). This principle of least privilege for Linux capabilities is the basis of Kubernetes security contexts.

weeks.title: Kubernetes, The Mental Model
weeks.context:
Kubernetes is the operating system for containers at scale. The core problem it solves: you have 10 containers (your app, the database, the cache, the background workers, the metrics collector) running across 5 servers. How do you decide which container runs on which server? How do you restart crashed containers? How do you update containers without downtime? How do you expose services on the network? Kubernetes answers all of these questions with a declarative API.

The key mental model: you tell Kubernetes what you want (desired state), and Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual state match the desired state. You do not say "start container X on server 3." You say "I want 3 replicas of container X." Kubernetes decides where to place them (the scheduler), starts them, monitors them, and restarts them if they crash (the controller manager).

The building blocks. Pod: the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers that share network and storage. Usually one container per pod. Deployment: manages a set of replicas of a pod. It ensures the desired number are running and handles rolling updates. Service: gives pods a stable network endpoint. Pods come and go (they restart, move to different nodes); a Service has a stable IP and DNS name that load-balances across the current pod set. ConfigMap: external configuration (non-sensitive) mounted as files or environment variables. Secret: sensitive configuration, encoded in base64 and stored in Kubernetes' etcd (with encryption at rest if configured).

Nodes and the control plane: a Kubernetes cluster has worker nodes (where your pods run) and the control plane (where the Kubernetes API server, scheduler, and controller manager run). kubectl communicates with the API server. The API server stores desired state in etcd. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes. The kubelet on each node pulls the assigned pods and runs them via containerd.

kubectl is your primary tool for interacting with Kubernetes: kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod [name], kubectl logs [pod-name], kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml, kubectl delete -f manifest.yaml. Everything in Kubernetes is defined in YAML manifests.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between a Pod and a Deployment? A Pod is a single instance of your application running in a container (or group of containers). If a Pod crashes, it is gone, Kubernetes does not automatically replace it (unless something else manages it). A Deployment is a controller that manages a set of Pod replicas. You specify replicas: 3 and the Deployment ensures 3 identical Pods are always running. If one crashes, the Deployment creates a replacement. When you update the image, the Deployment performs a rolling update (starts new Pods with the new image, terminates old ones, always maintaining a minimum number of running Pods during the update). Use Deployments for stateless applications. Use StatefulSets for stateful applications (databases) where each Pod has a stable identity and persistent storage.

mastery_questions: What is the difference between a Pod and a Deployment? A Pod is a single instance of your application running in a container (or group of containers). If a Pod crashes, it is gone, Kubernetes does not automatically replace it (unless something else manages it). A Deployment is a controller that manages a set of Pod replicas. You specify replicas: 3 and the Deployment ensures 3 identical Pods are always running. If one crashes, the Deployment creates a replacement. When you update the image, the Deployment performs a rolling update (starts new Pods with the new image, terminates old ones, always maintaining a minimum number of running Pods during the update). Use Deployments for stateless applications. Use StatefulSets for stateful applications (databases) where each Pod has a stable identity and persistent storage.

You have 3 replicas of your app Pod. A user makes a request. How does the request reach the correct Pod? A Service with selector: app: myapp matches all Pods with the label app: myapp. The Service gets a ClusterIP (a stable virtual IP within the cluster) and a DNS name (myapp.default.svc.cluster.local). kube-proxy on each node programs iptables rules that load-balance traffic to the ClusterIP across the 3 pod IPs (round-robin by default). When a Pod is replaced, its new IP is automatically added to the Service's endpoint list. The user's request hits the Service IP; iptables forwards it to one of the Pod IPs.

A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff status. What does this mean and how do you investigate? The container is crashing repeatedly. Kubernetes restarts it, but exponentially backs off between restarts (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s... up to 5 minutes). To investigate: kubectl logs [pod-name], see the last crash output. kubectl logs [pod-name] --previous, see the output from the previous crash (the container that crashed). kubectl describe pod [pod-name], see events (why the container started, what happened). The most common causes: incorrect environment variables (missing DATABASE_URL), the application crashing on startup due to a bug, or a misconfigured liveness probe that is killing the container before it finishes starting.

What is a Namespace in Kubernetes and why do you use them? A Namespace is a virtual cluster within a physical cluster. Resources (Pods, Deployments, Services) are isolated per namespace. The default namespace is default. Kubernetes system components run in kube-system. You create namespaces to separate environments (dev, staging, production) or teams (team-a, team-b) within the same physical cluster. Resource quotas can be applied per namespace (team-a can use at most 4 CPU and 8GB RAM). RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) can be scoped to namespaces (team-a members can only manage resources in the team-a namespace).

And a Service of type ClusterIP on port 80 targeting the Deployment."

weeks.pre_flight: Install kubectl: kubectl.io/docs/tasks/tools. Install minikube (for local Kubernetes): minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start. Start a local cluster: minikube start. Verify: kubectl cluster-info. Install k9s (TUI for Kubernetes): k9scli.io, much faster than typing kubectl commands. Read the Kubernetes concepts documentation: pods, deployments, services, and configmaps. Run kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods --all-namespaces to see the cluster state.
common_mistakes: Running stateful applications (databases) as simple Deployments. Deployments assume stateless pods, any pod can be replaced by any other pod. Databases need stable network identities (Pod 0 is the primary, Pod 1 is the replica) and stable persistent volumes. Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for databases. Or better: use managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) outside Kubernetes.

Not setting resource requests and limits on every container. Without requests, the scheduler cannot make good placement decisions (it does not know how much CPU/memory your container needs). Without limits, one container can consume all resources on a node and starve others. Set both for every container.

Using kubectl edit to make ad-hoc changes to running resources. Changes made with kubectl edit are not tracked in git and will be overwritten the next time you apply your manifests. Always make changes in your YAML files and apply them. kubectl edit is for emergency debugging only.

Not understanding the difference between kubectl apply and kubectl replace. apply is declarative and idempotent, it computes the difference between your manifest and the current state. replace replaces the entire resource. Use apply for normal operations. replace is for cases where apply cannot merge (rare). Never use kubectl create for resources you manage with manifests, it fails if the resource already exists.

Exposing a Service as NodePort for external access in production. NodePort opens a port on every node (30000-32767 range). This is fine for testing but not for production. Use a LoadBalancer Service (which provisions a cloud load balancer) or an Ingress controller for HTTP/HTTPS traffic.
weeks.debug_help: Pod is stuck in Pending: kubectl describe pod [name] > Events section. "0/2 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient memory" means the Pod's requested memory exceeds what any node has available. Reduce the resource request or add a node. Pod is in ImagePullBackOff: the container image cannot be pulled. Check the image name and tag. For private registries, check that the imagePullSecret is configured correctly. kubectl commands time out: check kubectl cluster-info, is the cluster reachable? For minikube, ensure minikube status shows the cluster is running. Service is not routing to Pods: check that the Service selector (matchLabels) matches the Pod labels exactly. kubectl get endpoints [service-name] shows which Pod IPs are in the endpoint list. If it is empty, the selector does not match.
stretch: Deploy a complete multi-tier application (web app + PostgreSQL + Redis) to your local minikube cluster. Use a Deployment for the web app, a StatefulSet for PostgreSQL, a Deployment for Redis, Services connecting them, ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, and Secrets for passwords. Expose the web app with a NodePort Service and access it in your browser.

Learn the Kubernetes RBAC system. Create a service account for a hypothetical CI system. Grant it permission to: get, list, watch Deployments in the production namespace, and update images in those Deployments. Restrict it from accessing Secrets. Test that it can update the Deployment but not read secrets with kubectl auth can-i.

Set up cluster monitoring on minikube: deploy the kube-prometheus-stack using Helm (covered next week). Access the Grafana dashboard and explore the default dashboards, node CPU/memory, Pod status, and the number of API server requests. This is a preview of W19's observability content.

weeks.title: Kubernetes in Production, Probes, Resources, HPA, Storage
weeks.context:
Running Kubernetes in development (W9) teaches the concepts. Running it in production teaches the hard lessons. Production Kubernetes requires four things that are unnecessary in local testing: probes (how the cluster knows your pod is healthy), resource management (how the scheduler places pods and prevents noisy neighbours), autoscaling (how the cluster handles traffic spikes without over-provisioning), and storage (how stateful applications persist data across pod restarts).

Probes: Kubernetes has three probe types. Liveness probe: "is the container still alive?" If this fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. Use for detecting deadlocks or unresponsive states. Readiness probe: "is the container ready to serve traffic?" If this fails, the pod is removed from the Service's endpoint list, it stops receiving traffic but is not restarted. Use for slow startup or temporary unavailability (running a database migration). Startup probe: "has the container started yet?" Delays the liveness probe for slow-starting applications. A misconfigured liveness probe that fires too early will kill healthy pods in a restart loop.

Resource requests and limits. Requests: what the scheduler guarantees each pod. The node must have at least this much free. Limits: the maximum a pod can use. On CPU: exceeding the limit causes throttling (the pod is slowed down). On memory: exceeding the limit causes an OOMKill (the pod is killed). The ratio between requests and limits is the resource "burstiness", a pod that requests 100m CPU but has a 1000m limit can burst 10x when resources are available.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): automatically scales the number of replicas based on CPU utilisation (or custom metrics). When average CPU usage across pods exceeds 70%, HPA adds more replicas. When it drops below 50%, HPA removes replicas. HPA requires the metrics-server add-on in minikube (minikube addons enable metrics-server).

PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims: the Kubernetes storage model. A PersistentVolume (PV) is a piece of storage provisioned by an admin or dynamically by a StorageClass. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage by a pod. The PVC binds to a PV of sufficient size and access mode. The pod mounts the PVC as a directory. When the pod restarts or moves to a different node (for RWO volumes, only possible within the same zone), the PVC follows.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a web application that takes 45 seconds to start (it runs database migrations on startup). You configure a liveness probe that checks /health every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3. What happens? The liveness probe starts immediately. After 30 seconds (3 failures × 10 seconds), Kubernetes determines the container is unhealthy and restarts it. The container restarts, takes another 45 seconds to start... and is killed again. This is a crash loop. The fix: add a startupProbe with failureThreshold: 60 and periodSeconds: 5 (total of 5 minutes for startup). The liveness probe is suspended until the startup probe succeeds. Once the app has started, liveness probe takes over.

mastery_questions: You have a web application that takes 45 seconds to start (it runs database migrations on startup). You configure a liveness probe that checks /health every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3. What happens? The liveness probe starts immediately. After 30 seconds (3 failures × 10 seconds), Kubernetes determines the container is unhealthy and restarts it. The container restarts, takes another 45 seconds to start... and is killed again. This is a crash loop. The fix: add a startupProbe with failureThreshold: 60 and periodSeconds: 5 (total of 5 minutes for startup). The liveness probe is suspended until the startup probe succeeds. Once the app has started, liveness probe takes over.

An HPA is configured to scale between 2 and 10 replicas, targeting 70% CPU. Current CPU is 40% with 3 replicas. The CPU suddenly spikes to 200%. What happens? HPA reacts within 30-60 seconds (the HPA sync interval). It calculates the desired replicas: ceil(3 × (200/70)) = ceil(8.57) = 9 replicas. It scales up to 9. The new pods take time to start (30-60 seconds for a typical Node app). During this window, the existing 3 pods handle 200% CPU (they are throttled). Once the 9 pods are ready, each handles 200/9 = 22% CPU (well below the 70% target). HPA will then scale down after the scale-down stabilisation window (5 minutes by default) to prevent flapping.

A StatefulSet pod is in Pending because "0/1 nodes are schedulable: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint". What is a taint and how do you fix it? A taint is a marker on a node that prevents pods from being scheduled there unless the pod has a matching toleration. Taints are used to reserve nodes for specific workloads: a GPU node might have a taint nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule. Only pods with a toleration for that taint can schedule there. To fix: either add a toleration to the pod spec (allows it to run on the tainted node), or identify a different untainted node for the pod. In minikube, the control plane node is often tainted NoSchedule, your workloads should run on worker nodes.

What is the difference between a PersistentVolume access mode ReadWriteOnce (RWO) and ReadWriteMany (RWX)? ReadWriteOnce: the volume can be mounted read-write by a single node at a time. All pods on that node can read and write, but pods on other nodes cannot mount it. This is typical for block storage (AWS EBS, GCP Persistent Disk). ReadWriteMany: the volume can be mounted read-write by multiple nodes simultaneously. Required for scenarios where multiple pods on different nodes need to read and write the same data (a shared file store). RWX requires a distributed filesystem: NFS, AWS EFS, Azure Files. Block storage does not support RWX.
ai_assist: "Write Kubernetes YAML for a Node.js Deployment with: a startup probe (GET /health, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5, allows 2.5 minutes for startup), a liveness probe (GET /health, after startup succeeds), and a readiness probe (GET /ready, which checks database connectivity). Set resource requests and limits appropriately for a typical Node web server."

"Write a HorizontalPodAutoscaler for a Deployment that scales between 2 and 20 replicas based on CPU utilisation (target 60%) and custom metric http_requests_per_second (target 100 rps). Include the scale-down stabilization window of 5 minutes to prevent flapping."

"Write a PersistentVolumeClaim and the corresponding volume mount in a Pod spec for a PostgreSQL StatefulSet. The PVC requests 10Gi of storage with ReadWriteOnce access mode and uses the default StorageClass. Mount it at /var/lib/postgresql/data."
weeks.pre_flight: Enable the metrics-server add-on in minikube: minikube addons enable metrics-server. Run kubectl top nodes and kubectl top pods to verify metrics are available. Read the Kubernetes documentation on probes, resource management, and HPA. Understand what QoS classes are in Kubernetes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort) and how they affect OOM kill priority.
common_mistakes: Setting the liveness probe to the same endpoint and timing as the readiness probe. They serve different purposes. The liveness probe should be lightweight (just checks if the process is alive). The readiness probe checks actual readiness (database connection). If the database goes down, the readiness probe should fail (removing the pod from the load balancer), but the liveness probe should continue to pass (do not restart the pod, the database is the problem, not the pod).

Not setting resource requests, which leads to Burstable or BestEffort QoS class. Pods without both requests and limits are BestEffort, the first to be OOM-killed when the node runs low on memory. Set both requests and limits on every container. Set them equal for predictable performance (Guaranteed QoS class).

Scaling down too aggressively. HPA's default scale-down behaviour removes one pod per minute. This is slow but prevents cascading failures. Do not set aggressively short stabilizationWindowSeconds on scale-down, a traffic spike that ends can cause premature scale-down, then another spike can overwhelm the under-provisioned fleet.

Using a Deployment with RWO PersistentVolumes for a stateful workload. If the pod is rescheduled to a different node, the EBS volume (RWO) cannot follow, it is in the old node's availability zone. Use a StatefulSet with PVCs for stateful workloads, and use storage in the same zone as the node.

Not setting PodDisruptionBudgets. When a node is drained (for maintenance, upgrade, or scaling down), Kubernetes evicts pods. Without a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), all pods of a Deployment could be evicted simultaneously, causing an outage. Set a PDB: minAvailable: 1 ensures at least one replica is always running during voluntary disruptions.
weeks.debug_help: HPA is not scaling: verify that metrics-server is running (kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server). HPA requires the metrics API. Check kubectl describe hpa [name] for events. HPA will not scale if the current metric is within the target range (it is working correctly). Pod is OOMKilled: kubectl describe pod [name] shows "OOMKilled" in the container state. Increase the memory limit or profile the application for memory leaks. PVC is stuck in Pending: kubectl describe pvc [name] for the reason. Common causes: no available PV that matches the size and access mode, or the StorageClass is not configured. In minikube, use storageClassName: standard.
stretch: Implement Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) alongside HPA. VPA recommends and optionally adjusts resource requests based on actual usage. Run it in recommendation mode (updateMode: Off) for one week and see what resource requests it recommends. This gives you data-driven resource sizing instead of guessing.

Deploy a chaos engineering experiment using chaos-mesh or litmus. Configure a pod failure experiment that randomly kills pods in your Deployment at 5-minute intervals. Verify that your HPA and pod restart policies keep the application serving traffic during the failures. This proves your resilience configuration works.

Set up cluster autoscaling in minikube using minikube's autoscaler profile. Configure the Cluster Autoscaler to add nodes when pods are unschedulable and remove empty nodes. Observe the full autoscaling chain: load spikes → HPA adds pods → pods are unschedulable → Cluster Autoscaler adds a node → pods schedule.

weeks.title: Helm and the K8s Package Ecosystem
weeks.context:
Raw Kubernetes YAML is verbose, repetitive, and hard to manage across environments. A Deployment manifest for your staging environment is almost identical to production, but with different image tags, replica counts, resource limits, and environment variables. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes that solves this problem.

A Helm chart is a collection of templates and default values. Templates are Kubernetes YAML files with Go template syntax for parameterisation: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} is replaced with the value from values.yaml. You install a chart with helm install myrelease ./mychart --set image.tag=1.2.3. Helm renders the templates with the provided values and sends the resulting YAML to Kubernetes.

Charts have a standard directory structure: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, description), values.yaml (default values), templates/ (YAML templates), charts/ (chart dependencies). The values.yaml contains sensible defaults; users override them with --set or custom values files (helm install -f prod-values.yaml).

The Helm chart repository ecosystem: Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io) hosts thousands of community charts. Adding a repository: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami. Installing a chart: helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret. This is how you deploy PostgreSQL, Redis, nginx, Prometheus, and many other services without writing any YAML yourself.

Helm vs Kustomize: Helm uses Go templates for parameterisation (powerful but complex, logic, loops, conditionals). Kustomize uses overlays (patch files that override specific fields). Kustomize is simpler for small differences between environments; Helm is more powerful for complex parameterisation. Many teams use Kustomize for their own applications and Helm for third-party software (databases, monitoring stacks).

Helm release management: helm list shows installed releases. helm history myrelease shows the history of changes. helm rollback myrelease 2 rolls back to revision 2. helm uninstall myrelease removes all resources the release created.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You are deploying a PostgreSQL database using the Bitnami Helm chart. The default values use a random password. You want to set a specific password for your environment and persist it across upgrades. How do you do this? Create a values override file prod-values.yaml with: auth: { postgresPassword: "your-secure-password" }. Install with: helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql -f prod-values.yaml. For upgrades (helm upgrade), pass the same -f prod-values.yaml. Alternatively: create a Kubernetes Secret manually before installing, and configure the chart to use the existing secret: auth: { existingSecret: "my-postgres-secret" }. This is the better production approach, the password is in a Secret managed by your secret management system, not in a values file.

mastery_questions: You are deploying a PostgreSQL database using the Bitnami Helm chart. The default values use a random password. You want to set a specific password for your environment and persist it across upgrades. How do you do this? Create a values override file prod-values.yaml with: auth: { postgresPassword: "your-secure-password" }. Install with: helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql -f prod-values.yaml. For upgrades (helm upgrade), pass the same -f prod-values.yaml. Alternatively: create a Kubernetes Secret manually before installing, and configure the chart to use the existing secret: auth: { existingSecret: "my-postgres-secret" }. This is the better production approach, the password is in a Secret managed by your secret management system, not in a values file.

You have written a Helm chart for your application. The chart has a template for a Service. In the template, you want to make the service type (ClusterIP, LoadBalancer, NodePort) configurable. Show the template syntax. In templates/service.yaml: apiVersion: v1, kind: Service, spec: { type: {{ .Values.service.type }} }. In values.yaml: service: { type: ClusterIP }. To override at install time: helm install myapp ./myapp --set service.type=LoadBalancer. The template renders the value from .Values. If the value is not provided (via --set or -f), Helm uses the default from values.yaml.

You install a Helm chart at version 3.5.0. A new chart version 3.6.0 is available with a critical security fix. How do you upgrade? helm repo update (refresh the chart repository index). helm upgrade my-postgres bitnami/postgresql --version 3.6.0 -f prod-values.yaml. Helm upgrades the running resources to match the new chart version. If the upgrade fails (misconfiguration, incompatible changes), helm rollback my-postgres to return to the previous revision. Always review the chart's CHANGELOG or release notes before upgrading.

What is the difference between helm install and helm upgrade --install? helm install creates a new release, it fails if a release with that name already exists. helm upgrade upgrades an existing release, it fails if the release does not exist. helm upgrade --install is idempotent: if the release does not exist, it installs; if it does, it upgrades. This is the correct command for CI/CD pipelines where you do not know whether the release was previously installed.

Use standard Helm template helpers (_helpers.tpl)."

"Show how to deploy the Bitnami PostgreSQL Helm chart in production with: a specific chart version, external secret for the password (existingSecret), persistence enabled (10Gi), replica count of 1, and custom resource limits. Include the helm upgrade --install command and a production values file."
"Explain Helm's hook system. What is a pre-install hook and a post-upgrade hook? Show a Helm hook that runs a database migration job before the application Deployment is upgraded."
weeks.pre_flight: Install Helm: helm.sh/docs/intro/install. Verify: helm version. Add the Bitnami chart repository: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update. Know the helm install, helm upgrade, helm list, helm rollback, and helm uninstall commands. Read the Helm getting started guide. Have your local Kubernetes cluster running (minikube start).
common_mistakes: Not specifying --version when installing charts in production. Without --version, Helm installs the latest version. The next time someone installs from scratch, they may get a different version. Pin the chart version: helm install myapp bitnami/myapp --version 12.3.4.

Storing helm values files with secrets in git. Values files with passwords, API keys, or tokens committed to git are security incidents waiting to happen. Use Helm Secrets (with SOPS) or pass secrets via --set from a CI secret, never in a committed values file.

Not using --atomic in CI deployments. helm upgrade without --atomic can leave resources in a partially upgraded state if an error occurs. --atomic rolls back automatically if the upgrade fails (within the timeout). Use: helm upgrade --atomic --timeout 5m.

Overusing Helm for everything. Helm shines for distributing complex third-party software (databases, monitoring). For your own simple application YAML (3 resources), Kustomize or plain kubectl apply is often simpler and less magic.

Not reviewing rendered templates before applying. helm template myapp ./myapp --set image.tag=1.2 renders the templates to stdout without installing. Review the output to catch template errors, missing values, or unexpected configurations before applying to the cluster.
weeks.debug_help: helm install fails with "Error: cannot re-use a release name": a release with that name already exists. Use helm upgrade --install or delete the old release with helm uninstall myapp. Template rendering error ("undefined variable"): run helm template to see the rendered output and the specific template error. Check that the value path in the template matches the key structure in values.yaml (case-sensitive). Chart values not being applied: verify the values file path is correct and the YAML syntax is valid. Use helm get values myapp to see what values are actually applied to a running release. Resources not being deleted on helm uninstall: by default, PersistentVolumeClaims are not deleted (to prevent accidental data loss). Add --cascade=orphan to see what resources would be orphaned, or delete PVCs manually after uninstall.
stretch: Publish your own Helm chart to GitHub Pages. Create a GitHub repository with your chart, use chart-releaser-action to package and publish it on every tag. Add the GitHub Pages URL as a Helm repo: helm repo add myrepo https://yourusername.github.io/myrepo. This is how open source Helm charts are distributed.

Use Helm Secrets with SOPS to encrypt sensitive values in your values files. SOPS encrypts specific keys in YAML using an AWS KMS key, GCP KMS key, or age key. The encrypted file is safe to commit to git. CI decrypts it at deploy time using the KMS key (accessed via IAM role). This is the production-grade solution for Helm values with secrets.

Migrate your Edge Portfolio application from raw kubectl YAML to a Helm chart. Parameterise: image tag, replica count, ingress hostname, and resource limits. Create a values-staging.yaml and values-production.yaml. Update your CI pipeline to use helm upgrade --install with the appropriate values file for each environment.

weeks.title: Service Mesh and Modern Networking, Istio, Linkerd, eBPF
weeks.context:
Kubernetes networking handles communication between pods and between the cluster and the outside world. But as applications grow more complex, microservices communicating with each other, diverse clients with different requirements, security policies between services, the basic Service and Ingress are not enough. Service meshes and modern networking tools fill this gap.

The service mesh problem: you have 50 microservices talking to each other. You want: mutual TLS (mTLS) between services (so a compromised service cannot spy on other services' traffic), traffic metrics (how many requests per second between service A and service B, what is the error rate), circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to a service that is failing), and gradual traffic shifting (send 5% of traffic to the new version before committing). Implementing all of this in each service's application code is duplicative and error-prone. A service mesh adds this as infrastructure, transparent to the application.

Istio: the most feature-rich service mesh. It injects a sidecar proxy (Envoy) into every pod. The sidecar intercepts all traffic in and out of the pod. Istio's control plane (istiod) configures the sidecars. From the application's perspective, nothing changes, it still makes HTTP requests to the Service. The sidecars handle mTLS, telemetry, and traffic policies transparently. The tradeoff: Istio is complex, resource-intensive (each sidecar adds ~50MB memory), and has a learning curve.

Linkerd: a lighter-weight service mesh focused on simplicity. Uses its own proxy (written in Rust, much lighter than Envoy). Provides mTLS, traffic metrics, and retries out of the box. Less feature-rich than Istio but significantly simpler to operate. The right choice if you want the core service mesh benefits without Istio's complexity.

eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter): a technology that allows you to run programs in the Linux kernel without modifying the kernel source or loading kernel modules. Cilium uses eBPF for Kubernetes networking: it replaces kube-proxy, provides high-performance networking, and can implement network policies and observability at the kernel level, without sidecar proxies. Cilium + Hubble (Cilium's observability component) provides service mesh-like capabilities without the sidecar overhead.

Kubernetes Ingress vs Gateway API: an Ingress routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to services. The Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor, it separates concerns between the infrastructure admin (Gateway), the cluster operator (Routes), and the developer (HTTPRoute). The Gateway API is the future of Kubernetes external traffic management.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Explain how Istio's mutual TLS (mTLS) works between two services without changing the application code. When service A wants to talk to service B, A's application code makes an HTTP request to B's Service DNS name. The Envoy sidecar in A's pod intercepts the outgoing request. It looks up the certificate for service B from istiod (Citadel, the Istio CA). It upgrades the connection to TLS, presents A's certificate to B's sidecar, and verifies B's certificate. B's sidecar verifies A's certificate and forwards the decrypted request to the service B application. The application never sees TLS, it makes plain HTTP internally. From outside the pod, all traffic is encrypted and authenticated.

mastery_questions: Explain how Istio's mutual TLS (mTLS) works between two services without changing the application code. When service A wants to talk to service B, A's application code makes an HTTP request to B's Service DNS name. The Envoy sidecar in A's pod intercepts the outgoing request. It looks up the certificate for service B from istiod (Citadel, the Istio CA). It upgrades the connection to TLS, presents A's certificate to B's sidecar, and verifies B's certificate. B's sidecar verifies A's certificate and forwards the decrypted request to the service B application. The application never sees TLS, it makes plain HTTP internally. From outside the pod, all traffic is encrypted and authenticated.

You want to gradually shift traffic from version 1 to version 2 of your service, 10% to v2, 90% to v1. After verifying v2 is healthy, shift to 50/50, then 100% to v2. How do you implement this with Istio? Create two Deployments: myservice-v1 with label version: v1 and myservice-v2 with label version: v2. Create a single Service that matches both (selector: app: myservice). Create a VirtualService that routes based on weight: destination: host: myservice, subset: v1, weight: 90 and subset: v2, weight: 10. The DestinationRule defines the subsets using pod labels. To update the weights, edit the VirtualService: kubectl apply changes take effect immediately, Istio's control plane pushes the new routing rules to all Envoy sidecars.

What is the difference between a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and Istio's AuthorizationPolicy? NetworkPolicy operates at the network layer (L3/L4, IP addresses and ports). It controls which pods can communicate with which other pods at the IP level. It is enforced by the CNI plugin (Cilium, Calico). AuthorizationPolicy operates at the application layer (L7, HTTP methods, paths, headers, service identity). It controls which services can call which endpoints. It is enforced by the Envoy sidecar. Example: a NetworkPolicy can say "only pods in namespace monitoring can reach port 9090." An AuthorizationPolicy can say "only the payments service (with its Istio identity certificate) can call POST /charge."

You are running Cilium as the CNI plugin and considering it as a replacement for Istio. What can Cilium with Hubble provide and what would you lose? Cilium + Hubble provides: network-level observability (which services are talking to which, traffic volume, error rates), network policies (L3/L4), and with Cilium Service Mesh: L7 observability and policies without sidecars. What you lose compared to Istio: Istio's rich traffic management features (VirtualService, DestinationRule, fault injection, retries, circuit breaking), Istio's mature mTLS with per-service certificate rotation, and the large Istio community and documentation. The tradeoff: Cilium is lower overhead (no sidecars), Istio is more feature-rich.

Include the two Deployments with version labels, the single Service selector, and the Istio traffic splitting configuration."

"Write a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that: allows all pods in the 'app' namespace to receive traffic only from pods with the label role: frontend, allows all pods to receive traffic from the 'monitoring' namespace on port 9090, and denies all other ingress traffic."

"Explain the Gateway API's resource model: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute. Compare it to the old Ingress resource. Show an HTTPRoute that routes traffic to different services based on the path prefix (/api to the API service, / to the frontend service) and adds a response header."
weeks.pre_flight: Install Istio on your minikube cluster: istioctl install --set profile=demo. Label the default namespace for sidecar injection: kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled. Deploy the sample application from the Istio documentation. Install Linkerd separately on a separate cluster or namespace to compare. Read the Istio concepts documentation (traffic management, security, observability).
common_mistakes: Installing Istio in production without understanding the resource requirements. Each sidecar adds 50-100MB RAM per pod. A cluster with 200 pods needs 10-20GB more RAM just for sidecars. Evaluate whether you need a service mesh before installing one. Many teams run successfully without a service mesh for years.

Enabling global mTLS in STRICT mode before verifying all services have sidecars. In STRICT mode, Istio rejects plain HTTP traffic. If any service does not have a sidecar (a pod that was created before enabling injection, or a job in a namespace without injection enabled), it cannot communicate. Start with PERMISSIVE mode, then switch to STRICT after verifying all traffic uses mTLS.

Not monitoring Istio's control plane resource usage. istiod, the Envoy proxies, and the Prometheus instance Istio installs consume significant resources. Set resource limits and monitor them. An OOM-killed istiod causes all sidecar proxies to fall back to cached config, which may be stale.

Using NetworkPolicy without Cilium or Calico. NetworkPolicy objects are only enforced if your CNI plugin supports them. The default kubenet and kindnet do not support NetworkPolicy. Without a supported CNI, NetworkPolicy objects are accepted by the API server but have no effect.

Forgetting to configure the ingress gateway. Istio replaces the standard nginx Ingress with an Istio Ingress Gateway. You must configure Gateway and VirtualService resources to route external traffic. Many teams set up Istio but forget to route external traffic through the Istio gateway.
weeks.debug_help: Sidecar not injected despite namespace label: check that the pod was created after the label was applied (existing pods do not get sidecars retroactively). Delete and recreate the pod. Service returns 503 after Istio installation: the sidecar is blocking traffic that was previously allowed. Check Istio's access logs (istioctl proxy-config log [pod] --level debug). mTLS failure: check the Istio authorization policy, if you have a DENY policy that inadvertently blocks legitimate traffic. Use kiali (Istio's UI) to visualise traffic and identify mTLS failures. Cilium pods in CrashLoopBackOff: Cilium requires specific kernel features. Check the minimum kernel version (4.9+ for basic, 5.3+ for full features). Use cilium status to see component health.
stretch: Deploy Kiali (Istio's service mesh observability UI) and explore the traffic graph for your sample application. Watch real-time traffic flow between services, see error rates and response times on each edge. Inject a fault (using Istio's fault injection) and watch how it propagates through the graph.

Implement zero-trust networking in your cluster: enable Istio mTLS in STRICT mode across all namespaces. Write AuthorizationPolicies for each service that specify exactly which other services can call it. Deny all by default, allow specific paths. This is the zero-trust networking model, no implicit trust, even inside the cluster.

Explore eBPF with Cilium: replace kube-proxy with Cilium's eBPF-based implementation (helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --set kubeProxyReplacement=strict). Use Hubble to observe the real-time network flows. Compare the latency of kube-proxy iptables rules vs Cilium eBPF using a simple benchmark (hey or wrk).

weeks.title: Terraform, Infrastructure as Code Done Right
weeks.context:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means your infrastructure is defined in version-controlled files, just like your application code. Before IaC: you click through a cloud console to create a VPC, subnets, security groups, EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers. The configuration exists only in the cloud provider's database. There is no record of why you made each decision. Recreating it in another region takes hours and is error-prone. After IaC with Terraform: your entire infrastructure is in .tf files. Recreating it is terraform apply. Auditing is git blame.

Terraform is the dominant IaC tool. It uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), a declarative syntax that describes desired infrastructure state. Providers connect Terraform to cloud APIs: AWS, GCP, Azure, Cloudflare, GitHub, Datadog, and hundreds more. Terraform talks to the provider APIs to create, update, and delete resources.

The Terraform workflow. terraform init: downloads providers and modules. terraform plan: shows what changes will be made (resources to create, update, or destroy) without making them. Always review the plan. terraform apply: makes the changes. terraform destroy: tears down all resources. The plan/apply separation is Terraform's safety net, you see what will happen before it happens.

State: Terraform maintains a state file (terraform.tfstate) that maps your configuration to real cloud resources. The state is how Terraform knows what exists and what needs to change. Problem: the state file contains sensitive values (database passwords, API keys) and must be stored securely and shared across team members. Solution: remote state in S3 (with DynamoDB for state locking) or Terraform Cloud. Never commit terraform.tfstate to git.

Modules: reusable Terraform configurations. A module encapsulates a set of resources and exposes input variables and output values. The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) has community modules for common patterns: VPCs, EKS clusters, RDS instances. Instead of writing 200 lines of AWS VPC configuration, use the terraform-aws-vpc module with a few variables.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You change the instance_type of an existing EC2 instance in your Terraform configuration from t3.micro to t3.small. You run terraform plan. What does the plan show, and what happens to the running instance? Terraform shows: "aws_instance.web will be updated in-place" with instance_type changing from t3.micro to t3.small. For most EC2 changes, Terraform stops the instance, modifies it, and restarts it, brief downtime. However, for some changes (like changing the AMI), Terraform must destroy and recreate the instance: "aws_instance.web must be replaced", it creates the new instance and destroys the old one. Read the plan carefully for "must be replaced" vs "updated in-place" to understand the impact.

mastery_questions: You change the instance_type of an existing EC2 instance in your Terraform configuration from t3.micro to t3.small. You run terraform plan. What does the plan show, and what happens to the running instance? Terraform shows: "aws_instance.web will be updated in-place" with instance_type changing from t3.micro to t3.small. For most EC2 changes, Terraform stops the instance, modifies it, and restarts it, brief downtime. However, for some changes (like changing the AMI), Terraform must destroy and recreate the instance: "aws_instance.web must be replaced", it creates the new instance and destroys the old one. Read the plan carefully for "must be replaced" vs "updated in-place" to understand the impact.

Your team has two engineers working with the same Terraform state. Engineer A runs terraform apply while Engineer B is also running terraform apply. What happens without state locking, and how does state locking solve this? Without locking: both plans are based on the same state snapshot. Both applies run concurrently. The second apply may corrupt the state (race condition on the state file write) or create duplicate resources. With state locking: when Engineer A runs terraform apply, Terraform acquires a lock on the remote state (using DynamoDB for S3 backend). Engineer B's apply finds the lock, waits, and retries. After Engineer A's apply completes and releases the lock, Engineer B's apply proceeds, using the updated state as its baseline.

You accidentally delete a resource from your Terraform configuration and run terraform apply. Terraform deletes the corresponding cloud resource. The database is gone. How do you recover? If you have backups (AWS RDS automated backups, S3 versioning), restore from backup. For the Terraform state: you can import the restored resource back into state: terraform import aws_db_instance.main [restored-instance-id]. This tells Terraform that the restored resource corresponds to the aws_db_instance.main configuration block. Then restore the configuration block. Prevent recurrence: set lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources, Terraform will refuse to destroy them even when you remove them from configuration (you get an error instead of accidental deletion).

What is the difference between Terraform plan output of "~" (tilde) and "-/+" (dash plus)? Tilde (~) means the resource will be updated in-place, the existing resource is modified without recreation. Example: changing an EC2 instance's tags. Dash plus (-/+) means the resource will be destroyed and recreated, the change cannot be applied in-place. Example: changing an EC2 instance's AMI. The old resource is marked for destruction (-) and a new one is marked for creation (+). Always understand which resources are recreated in a plan, it determines the blast radius of a Terraform change.

Use the eu-west-1 region."

"Write a Terraform module for a Kubernetes namespace with associated RBAC. The module creates a Namespace, a ServiceAccount, a Role with read-only access to pods and deployments, and a RoleBinding. The module takes namespace_name and team_name as input variables."

"Set up a Terraform remote backend using AWS S3 and DynamoDB state locking. Show the backend configuration block, the S3 bucket policy (deny non-HTTPS access, enable versioning, enable server-side encryption), and the DynamoDB table for locking. weeks.pre_flight: Install Terraform: developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install. Verify: terraform version. Create an AWS account or use an existing one. Create an IAM user with programmatic access and the permissions you need. Configure AWS credentials: aws configure (or use environment variables). Create an S3 bucket and DynamoDB table for remote state (terraform backend). Read the Terraform "Get Started - AWS" guide on HashiCorp's developer portal.
common_mistakes: Running terraform apply without reviewing the plan. terraform apply shows the plan before applying but many developers skip reading it. Run terraform plan first, save it to a file (terraform plan -out=tfplan), review it, then apply only the saved plan (terraform apply tfplan).

Storing terraform.tfstate in git. State files contain sensitive values (passwords, private keys, access tokens) in plaintext. Use remote state (S3 + DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud). If you accidentally commit state, rotate all credentials immediately.

Not using provider version constraints. Without version constraints, terraform init downloads the latest provider version. A provider update can introduce breaking changes. Pin provider versions: required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" } }.

Writing monolithic Terraform configurations. One giant main.tf with 2000 lines is hard to review and has large blast radius (a mistake can affect everything). Separate by concern: networking.tf, compute.tf, database.tf. Or use modules for reusable components.

Not using terraform fmt and terraform validate. fmt formats your HCL consistently (like gofmt). validate checks for syntax errors and obvious mistakes. Run both before committing. Add them to your CI pipeline.
weeks.debug_help: "Error: state file is locked": another terraform apply is in progress (or a previous apply was interrupted). Check DynamoDB for the lock record: aws dynamodb scan --table-name terraform-locks. If the lock is stale, delete it (terraform force-unlock [lock-id]). "Error: Reference to undeclared resource": you reference a resource that does not exist in your configuration (typo in resource name, or you removed it). Check the resource type and name match. "Provider configuration not present": you removed a provider block but there are still resources from that provider. Remove the resources first, apply, then remove the provider. Terraform plan shows unexpected changes: you manually changed a cloud resource outside of Terraform. The plan will show Terraform "fixing" the drift by reverting your manual change. Use terraform import to bring manual changes into state, or accept the revert.
stretch: Implement Terraform CI/CD with Atlantis (the open-source tool for Terraform pull request automation). Atlantis runs on a server and comments on PRs with terraform plan output. Merging the PR automatically runs terraform apply. This gives your team a peer-reviewed, audited infrastructure change process.

Write a Terratest (go test-based infrastructure testing) for your Terraform module. The test applies the module, verifies the created resources are accessible (HTTP check on the EC2 instance, connection check on the database), and destroys the resources. This is infrastructure TDD.

Migrate your Edge Portfolio infrastructure (server, DNS, SSL) to Terraform. Write resources for: DigitalOcean Droplet, Cloudflare DNS records, and a null_resource that configures nginx and SSL via SSH. Verify that terraform destroy and terraform apply recreate the identical infrastructure from scratch.

weeks.title: Managed Kubernetes, EKS, GKE, AKS
weeks.context:
Managed Kubernetes services (EKS on AWS, GKE on Google Cloud, AKS on Azure) eliminate the burden of managing the Kubernetes control plane. In a self-managed cluster, you are responsible for: etcd backups, API server certificate rotation, control plane version upgrades, master node high availability, and more. With a managed service, the cloud provider handles all of that. You pay for the worker nodes; the control plane is managed.

EKS (Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service): AWS manages the control plane. You provision worker nodes (EC2 instances) in node groups, or use Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage, pods run directly). EKS integrates with AWS services: IAM for authentication (IRSA, IAM Roles for Service Accounts, letting pods assume IAM roles without long-lived credentials), ALB (Application Load Balancer) for Ingress, EBS/EFS for PersistentVolumes.

GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine): Google's managed Kubernetes. Often regarded as the most polished managed Kubernetes experience, GKE invented the technology after all. Features: Autopilot mode (GKE manages both control plane and nodes, fully managed), binary authorisation (only signed container images can run), and seamless integration with Cloud Run for serverless workloads.

AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service): Microsoft's offering. Strong integration with Azure Active Directory for authentication and Azure Monitor for observability. Popular in enterprise environments where Microsoft products dominate.

eksctl is the official CLI for EKS: eksctl create cluster --name myapp --region us-east-1 creates a complete EKS cluster. For production, use Terraform (terraform-aws-eks module) to manage the cluster as IaC. The eksctl approach is good for learning; Terraform is right for production.

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): the secure way to give Kubernetes pods access to AWS services. Instead of mounting long-lived AWS credentials into pods (security risk), IRSA lets pods assume an IAM role via a Kubernetes Service Account. The mechanism: an OIDC identity provider in your EKS cluster, an IAM role with a trust policy that allows the service account, and an annotation on the Kubernetes Service Account. Pods in that service account automatically receive temporary credentials for the IAM role.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You deploy an application to EKS that needs to read from an S3 bucket. How do you grant access securely without hardcoding AWS credentials? Use IRSA. Create an IAM role with a policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket. The trust policy allows the EKS cluster's OIDC provider to assume the role, restricted to a specific namespace and service account. Create a Kubernetes ServiceAccount in the namespace with the annotation: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/my-role. Use this ServiceAccount in your pod spec. The pod's containers receive temporary AWS credentials from the EKS pod identity webhook. No AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID needed.

mastery_questions: You deploy an application to EKS that needs to read from an S3 bucket. How do you grant access securely without hardcoding AWS credentials? Use IRSA. Create an IAM role with a policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket. The trust policy allows the EKS cluster's OIDC provider to assume the role, restricted to a specific namespace and service account. Create a Kubernetes ServiceAccount in the namespace with the annotation: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/my-role. Use this ServiceAccount in your pod spec. The pod's containers receive temporary AWS credentials from the EKS pod identity webhook. No AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID needed.

What is the difference between an EKS managed node group and Fargate? Managed node group: EC2 instances you provision and manage (choose instance type, AMI, size). Kubernetes schedules pods onto these nodes. You pay for the EC2 instances. You manage node upgrades (roll the AMI). Good for: predictable workloads, stateful applications, GPU workloads, cost optimisation (spot instances). Fargate: AWS runs each pod on dedicated compute, no EC2 nodes to manage. Each pod gets its own isolated micro-VM. You pay per pod per second. Good for: batch workloads, infrequent jobs, if you want truly managed infrastructure. Limitation: Fargate does not support DaemonSets, stateful sets with persistent volumes (certain storage drivers), or privileged containers.

How does EKS authentication work? Who can access your cluster and how? EKS uses IAM for authentication and Kubernetes RBAC for authorisation. The kube-apiserver does not natively speak IAM, it uses the AWS IAM Authenticator. When you run kubectl, the kubeconfig executes aws eks get-token which calls the STS AssumeRole API and returns a short-lived token. The API server passes the token to the IAM Authenticator which validates it with AWS. The IAM Authenticator maps the IAM principal (user or role) to a Kubernetes username and groups, defined in the aws-auth ConfigMap (or now, EKS Access Entries). Kubernetes RBAC then determines what the username/groups can do.

An EKS cluster is running in us-east-1. You want pods to communicate with an RDS database in the same VPC. How do you configure networking? The EKS worker nodes run in your VPC (you specified the subnets when creating the node group). The RDS database is also in the VPC (in private subnets). The pods inherit the worker node's VPC connectivity, they can reach the RDS endpoint by its DNS name within the VPC (no internet required). The security group on the RDS database must allow inbound traffic on port 5432 from the worker node security group (or the pod IP range if using custom networking). Connection string: use the RDS endpoint hostname, which resolves to a private VPC IP.

weeks.stakeholder_moment: EKS cluster audience is the on-call engineer at 3am + the security auditor + the CFO. The on-call needs: every alert names the runbook. The auditor needs: every change in audit log. The CFO needs: every dollar tagged.
weeks.pre_flight: Create an AWS account with billing set up. Install eksctl: eksctl.io/installation. Install the AWS CLI: aws.amazon.com/cli. Configure credentials: aws configure with your IAM access key. Read the EKS getting started guide. Know that an EKS cluster costs money, a minimal cluster (control plane + 2 t3.micro nodes) costs about $0.10/hour for the control plane plus EC2 costs. Destroy the cluster when not in use.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to delete the cluster when not using it. EKS costs money even when idle (control plane: $0.10/hour, worker nodes: EC2 instance costs). Set a calendar reminder or use AWS Cost Alerts. Use eksctl delete cluster or terraform destroy when done learning.

Placing all worker nodes in public subnets. Production workloads should run in private subnets. Public subnets have direct internet routes, not necessary for worker nodes (they egress via a NAT gateway). Use private subnets for nodes, public subnets for load balancers only.

Using the cluster admin kubeconfig in production applications. The kubeconfig that eksctl creates has admin privileges. Use IRSA for pod-to-AWS communication. Use Kubernetes Service Accounts with scoped RBAC for pod-to-Kubernetes communication. Never mount admin kubeconfig into pods.

Not configuring the cluster autoscaler. Without the Cluster Autoscaler, your EKS cluster has a fixed number of nodes. When pods are unschedulable (not enough node capacity), they remain pending. The Cluster Autoscaler watches for pending pods and adds nodes (and removes empty nodes). This is separate from HPA (which scales pods), CA scales nodes.

Ignoring EKS version end-of-life. EKS supports Kubernetes for approximately 14 months per minor version. After end-of-life, no security patches are applied. Plan for version upgrades: test in a staging cluster, upgrade the control plane first (managed by AWS), then the node groups.
weeks.debug_help: kubectl cannot connect to the cluster: run aws eks update-kubeconfig --name CLUSTER --region REGION to update your kubeconfig. Check that your IAM user/role is in the aws-auth ConfigMap. eks:DescribeCluster permission is required. Pod cannot reach RDS: check the RDS security group, does it allow the worker node security group as a source? Run kubectl exec into a pod and nc -zv RDS_ENDPOINT 5432 to test connectivity. ALB Ingress controller not working: ensure the AWS Load Balancer Controller is installed (check helm list -n kube-system). Check the ALB controller logs. The controller needs IRSA permissions to create ALBs. Nodes in NotReady state: kubectl describe node [node-name] for the reason. Common causes: EC2 instance health check failure (replace the node), kubelet failing to connect to the API server (check security groups and VPC routing), or disk pressure (node has insufficient disk space).
stretch: Set up GitOps for your EKS cluster using Flux CD (covered further in W18). Flux watches a git repository and automatically applies changes to the cluster. When you push a new Kubernetes manifest or change an image tag, Flux reconciles the cluster state. This closes the loop between code changes and cluster state.

Implement cost optimisation on your EKS cluster using Karpenter (the newer, more efficient replacement for the Cluster Autoscaler). Karpenter provisions nodes directly (bypassing auto-scaling groups) and can select the optimal instance type for each pod's requirements. Configure Spot instances for interruptible workloads.

Deploy a multi-region active-passive setup: EKS in us-east-1 (primary) and eu-west-1 (secondary). Use Route 53 health checks to fail over DNS from the primary to the secondary if the primary's health check fails. Use RDS cross-region read replicas that can be promoted to primary during a failover.

weeks.title: Multi-Cloud, Vendor Lock-in, and Picking Your Platform
weeks.context:
Every cloud provider has different APIs, different pricing models, different service names, and different strengths. AWS has the broadest service catalogue. GCP has the best Kubernetes and data engineering services. Azure is dominant in enterprise environments with Microsoft licenses. Choosing a cloud provider (or using multiple) is a significant architectural decision.

Vendor lock-in is the state where you depend on a specific vendor's proprietary services to the point where switching is prohibitively expensive. The opposite of lock-in is portability, running the same workload on any cloud or on-premises. The tension: proprietary managed services (AWS Lambda, GCP BigQuery, Azure Cosmos DB) offer significantly better developer experience and operational leverage than self-managed open source equivalents, but they tie you to a vendor.

The lock-in spectrum. High lock-in: using AWS Lambda (serverless, AWS-specific), DynamoDB (NoSQL, AWS-specific), SageMaker (ML platform). Low lock-in: running containerised applications on Kubernetes (portable across managed Kubernetes services and on-premises), PostgreSQL (runs everywhere), S3-compatible object storage (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2). The pragmatic approach: use proprietary services where the operational leverage is worth the lock-in. Avoid proprietary services for core data storage where migration cost is highest.

Multi-cloud: running workloads across multiple cloud providers simultaneously. The reasons: regulatory requirements (data must stay in a specific region where only one provider has a data centre), avoiding single-vendor risk, negotiating leverage. The reality: multi-cloud adds significant operational complexity. Most startup and mid-size companies do not need multi-cloud. If you are using Kubernetes, you are already 80% of the way to cloud-portable, the remaining 20% is storage, networking, and cloud-specific services.

Cloud-native vs cloud-agnostic: cloud-native means using the managed services of a specific cloud to their fullest extent (Lambda + DynamoDB + SQS + SNS + RDS + ...). Cloud-agnostic means running only portable workloads (containers on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Redis) that could run on any cloud. The pragmatic answer for most teams: be cloud-native for your chosen cloud (pick one and use it well) and accept the lock-in as a reasonable operational tradeoff.
